pl-l1d1.summary: Opening distinction of the Sentences, setting the framework for the whole work and for Book 1. Following Augustine's De doctrina christiana, all teaching concerns things or signs, so the work will treat things first and signs (the sacraments) last (c1). Things are divided into those to be enjoyed, those to be used, and those that enjoy and use; only the eternal, unchangeable Trinity is to be enjoyed and the world is to be used (c2). Lombard then resolves three difficulties by harmonizing Augustine with himself and with Ambrose: enjoyment in this life is real but imperfect; humans are to be loved for God's sake and not enjoyed, even oneself, and God 'uses' us for our good; and virtues, though loved for their own sake, are referred to beatitude, so we use them and through them enjoy God (c3). He closes by announcing the treatment of the Trinity.
claims: Sacred doctrine is concerned with things and signs, and treats things first.
Things are to be enjoyed, to be used, or are those that enjoy and use.
Only the Trinity, the eternal and unchangeable supreme good, is to be enjoyed; the world is to be used.
We enjoy God imperfectly in this life and fully in the next.
Humans, including oneself, are to be loved for God's sake, not enjoyed.
God does not enjoy us but uses us for our benefit and his goodness.
Virtues are loved for their own sake and yet referred to beatitude; through them we enjoy God.

pl-l1d2.summary: Begins the treatise on the Trinity. Lombard states the faith that the Trinity is the one true God, of one substance, approached only by purified minds and with modesty, since error here is most dangerous (c1), and sets out the Catholic teaching of unity of essence and plurality of persons, other in person (alius) but not in thing (aliud) (c2). He adopts Augustine's method: first scriptural authority, then reasons and similitudes against contentious reasoners (c3). He then collects Old Testament testimonies to unity (the Shema, 'I am who am'), to plurality and unity together (Gen 1:26, Elohim, the Trisagion), to the Son's eternal generation, and to the Spirit, drawing from Hilary the principle that number words in God remove solitude rather than posit something (c4). New Testament testimonies follow (baptismal formula, John 10:30, Rom 11:36) before he turns to reasons (c5).
claims: The Trinity is the one true God, of one substance or essence.
Inquiry into the Trinity requires modesty, purity of mind, and charitable correction.
There is unity of essence and plurality of persons; the persons are alius, not aliud.
The doctrine is to be shown first from Scripture, then defended by reasons and similitudes.
Both Testaments attest the unity of nature and the trinity of persons.
Numerical terms in God remove singularity and solitude rather than positing something.
Scripture attests the eternal generation of the Son and the divinity of the Holy Spirit.

pl-l1d3.summary: Moves from authorities to reasons and likenesses for the Trinity. From Rom 1:20 and Augustine's account of the philosophers, God can be known from creatures as the unchangeable, simple principle of all, eternal, omnipotent, wise, and good, and creatures bear a vestige of the Trinity in unity, form, and order; yet without revelation the Trinity cannot be sufficiently known (c1). The image of the Trinity is found in the mind: memory, understanding, and will are one life, mind, and essence, three by relation, mutually comprehending and equal. Lombard explains that they are 'one substance' in that they exist substantially in the soul, not as accidents (c2). He insists on the great unlikeness within the likeness: a man has these three but is not them and is one person, whereas God is three persons. He gives a second triad, mind, knowledge, and love, as parent, offspring, and proceeding love, and shows the mind ascending to one God with begotten wisdom and love (c3). The distinction ends by restating the faith: one nature, three related persons, the Father begetting, the Son born, the Spirit proceeding from both (c4).
claims: God's existence and attributes are knowable from creatures.
Creatures bear a vestige of the Trinity in unity, species, and order.
Sufficient knowledge of the Trinity requires revelation.
The human mind is an image of the Trinity in memory, understanding, and will, and in mind, knowledge, and love.
The mind is God's image chiefly because it can know and love God.
The image is marked by great unlikeness as well as likeness.
There is one divine nature and three persons, distinguished by begetting, being born, and proceeding.

pl-l1d4.summary: Treats the logic of 'God begot God.' Lombard grants that God the Father begot God the Son ('God from God') but denies both that God begot himself (nothing begets itself) and that he begot another God (God is one). He disarms the dilemma 'he begot a God who is or is not God the Father' by distinguishing personal from essential readings (c1). Against those who allow 'the three persons are one God' but not the converse, he shows from Augustine that the predication runs both ways: one God is the Trinity. He reads Augustine's 'begot another himself' as another person, not another thing (c2).
claims: 'God begot God' is true, since God the Father begot God the Son.
God neither begot himself nor another God.
The Son is God who is not the Father, yet not a God other than the God the Father is.
The three persons are one God, and one God is the three persons.
Father and Son are other persons (alius) but not other things (aliud).
concepts: convertible predication of essence and person

pl-l1d5.summary: Asks whether the Father begot the divine essence, the essence begot the Son, or essence begot essence, and denies all three. Generation would make the essence relative, something would beget itself, and, on Augustine's argument from wisdom, the begotten would cause the begetter's being, since in God to be is to be wise. Lombard then works through many seemingly contrary authorities: Augustine's 'begot what he is,' 'wisdom from wisdom, essence from essence'; Hilary's language of nature begotten and begetting; and Augustine against Maximinus that the Son is 'of the Father's substance.' Admitting he would rather hear than teach, he reads them personally: the Son, who is the same essence, is from the Father, who is that essence (c1). So the Son and Spirit are not from nothing or from matter, and formulas such as 'God from God, light from light, essence from essence' mean consubstantial and not the same person (c2). Hence only the only-begotten is Son by nature (c3).
claims: The Father did not beget the divine essence, the essence did not beget the Son, and essence did not beget essence.
What is said relatively does not signify substance.
In God's simplicity, to be and to be wise are the same.
Formulas like 'begot what he is,' 'substance from substance,' and 'of the Father's substance' are to be read personally: the Son, who is the same essence, is from the Father.
The Son and Spirit are neither from nothing nor from matter.
One says three persons 'of one essence,' not 'from' it.
Only the only-begotten is Son by nature.

pl-l1d6.summary: Asks whether the Father begot the Son by will or by necessity. With Augustine and Orosius: neither, for there is no necessity in God and will cannot precede wisdom. Against Eunomius's 'Son of will,' which implies a new will in a changeable God, the Son is Son by nature, as the Catholic retort ('Is the Father God willingly?') shows. To the objection that will and nature are identical, Lombard replies that identical attributes need not share all predicates, since God knows evil but wills only good. He concludes that the Father begot not by an antecedent will but willingly, as he begot wisely, and Hilary anathematizes both compulsion and generation against the Father's will (c1).
claims: The Father did not beget by antecedent will or by necessity.
The Son is Son by nature, not by will.
Positing a will that accrues to God makes God mutable.
Identical divine attributes are not interchangeable in all predications.
God's knowledge covers good and evil, his will only good.
The Father begot the Son willingly, as he begot wisely and powerfully, without a preceding will.

pl-l1d7.summary: Addresses arguments that power and will to beget would make the Father greater than the Son. Being able or willing to beget is not being able or willing 'something' subject to divine power, since the generation is eternal and above all things, and being Father is not being 'something' (c1). Lombard reluctantly takes up Augustine's reply to Maximinus that the Son 'was not unable but it was not fitting' to beget, reading it as saying that the Son's not begetting comes not from impotence but from his personal property of nativity. Then (c2) he holds that the Father is powerful only by nature, his power being his essence. The Son has the very same power by which the Father begets and the Son is begotten; Father and Son differ in property or notion, not in power or will.
claims: Being able to beget the Son is not being able to do something subject to power.
The Son's generation is eternal and above all things.
The Son's not begetting arises from his personal property, not from impotence.
God's power is his essence.
Father and Son have one and the same power and will.
Father and Son differ by properties or notions, not by power.

pl-l1d8.summary: Treats the truth, immutability, and simplicity of the divine essence. God is essence, named from 'to be' ('I am who am'), and alone properly is, without past or future. Verbs of every tense may be said of him, but they signify his simple existence without temporal motion (c1). God alone is properly unchangeable, receiving no accidents, so he alone 'has immortality'; every change is a kind of death, and creaturely impeccability comes by grace (c2). God alone is truly simple: bodies have parts and separable accidents, and the soul, though whole in every part, has varied qualities and is changeable (c3–4). God's many names signify one thing, since in him being is being wise or just (c5); the categories do not fit him, since he is good without quality and great without quantity (c6); and he is called 'substance' only loosely, since he underlies no accidents, while 'essence' is proper (c7). In God the haver and what is had are the same, yet this simplicity admits a Trinity of persons, distinguished only by what is said relatively (c8).
claims: God alone is properly essence or being, without past or future.
Tensed verbs predicated of God signify simple existence, not temporal motion.
God alone is properly immutable, and true immortality is immutability.
Every change in creatures is a kind of death; creaturely impeccability is by grace.
No creature is truly simple; God is supremely simple.
God's many names signify one divine nature; in God to be is to be wise, just, good.
The categories do not properly apply to God, who is subject to no accidents.
God is called substance improperly and essence properly.
In God the haver is what is had, except for the relative distinctions among persons.

pl-l1d9.summary: Turns to the distinction of persons, beginning with the Son's relation to the Father. The three are one God yet personally other (c1). The Son, though begotten, is coeternal: against the Arian 'if born, then there was when he was not,' Augustine argues from brightness and fire and from the Son as God's eternal wisdom, and Ambrose from the correlation of Father and Son and from divine immutability (c2). The manner of the generation is ineffable; we may know that he is born but not how (c3). On whether to say the Son 'is always being born' or 'is always born,' Lombard reconciles Gregory, Augustine, and Origen: 'always born' is more fitting, but 'always being born' is true of an eternal, not repeated, nativity. The Son is coeternal with the Father, his author, and with Hilary there is no interval between generation and nativity (c4). Against the objection that what is born was not always, the eternal Father always has the Son, a truth held by faith beyond reason (c5).
claims: The three persons are one God, yet personally distinct.
The Son is begotten and coeternal with the Father.
Since the Son is God's wisdom and God was never without wisdom, the Son is eternal.
Father and Son are correlatives, so the Father was always Father.
The manner of eternal generation is ineffable and not to be scrutinized.
'Always born' is the most fitting expression; 'always being born' is true of eternal nativity.
The Father is eternal without author; the Son is coeternal with his author.

pl-l1d10.summary: Begins the treatment of the Holy Spirit as the love of the Father and Son. With Augustine, charity, like wisdom, is said of each person and of the whole Trinity as one, yet is properly said of the Spirit, as wisdom is of the Son. So 'charity' sometimes names the common substance and sometimes the Spirit (c1). By the general rule that terms have common and proper uses, and by Augustine's exegesis of 1 John 4 (the love that is God from God, by which we abide in God), the Spirit is the love by which Father and Son love each other: the bond, communion, and charity, consubstantial and coeternal. Whether the Spirit is also the charity by which we love God is deferred to d. 17 (c2). The Spirit properly bears the names common to Father and Son ('spirit,' 'holy,' 'charity') as their communion, but he is not the only charity in God, otherwise the Son would be 'Son of the Spirit' (c3).
claims: The Holy Spirit is the love or charity of the Father and the Son.
Charity is said of each person and the whole Trinity, but properly of the Spirit.
Many terms have both general and proper uses in Trinitarian theology.
The Spirit is the bond and communion by which Father and Son love each other.
The love that is God from God in 1 John 4 is the Holy Spirit.
The Spirit properly bears names common to Father and Son.
The Spirit is not the only charity in God.

pl-l1d11.summary: Defends the procession of the Holy Spirit from both Father and Son against the Greeks. Scripture calls the Spirit the Spirit of the Father and of the Son and says both send him. The Greeks object that Christ names only the Father (John 15:26) and that the conciliar creeds, including the one Leo III inscribed in silver, forbid teaching 'otherwise' and lack the Filioque. Lombard replies that 'otherwise' means 'contrary,' not 'in addition,' and that Christ did not say 'from the Father alone' (c1). The Greeks agree in substance, since they confess the Spirit to be the Son's, which is the same as being from him, and Greek doctors such as Athanasius, Didymus, Cyril, and Chrysostom teach procession from the Son (c2).
claims: The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.
Scripture calls the Spirit the Spirit of both and says both send him.
The creedal anathema forbids contrary teaching, not addition.
Christ's 'proceeds from the Father' does not exclude the Son.
The Greeks agree in meaning, though not in words, since being the Spirit of the Son is being from the Son.
Greek fathers themselves taught procession from the Son.

pl-l1d12.summary: Answers two questions about the order of procession. Did the Spirit proceed from the Father before the Son? With Augustine, there are no intervals of time in the Trinity, so the procession is as timeless as the generation (c1). Does he proceed more fully from the Father? No. Augustine's 'principally' and Jerome's 'properly' from the Father mean that the Father has from himself, and the Son from the Father, that the Spirit proceeds from them. Hilary's 'from the Father through the Son' marks the Father's authority, not the Son's inferiority. This is why Christ named only the Father: as the Father timelessly gave the Son life in himself, he gave him to be the source of the Spirit (c2).
claims: The Spirit does not proceed from the Father before the Son; there is no time in the Trinity.
The Spirit does not proceed more fully from the Father than from the Son.
'Principally' and 'properly from the Father' mean that the Father has from himself what the Son has from the Father.
The Son received in his generation that the Spirit proceeds from him.
'Through the Son' expresses the Father's authority, not inferiority of the Son.

pl-l1d13.summary: Asks why the Spirit, who is from the Father, is not born or a son. If begotten by both he would be son of both, which is absurd (c1). Son and Spirit both proceed from the Father, but the Son by being born and the Spirit as given, as Gift; so the Spirit is neither a natural nor an adopted son (c2). With Augustine, we cannot in this life distinguish generation from procession: all that is born proceeds but not all that proceeds is born, and the procession, like the generation, is ineffable (c3). The Spirit should be called neither begotten nor unbegotten, since 'unbegotten' (not from another) belongs only to the Father; Jerome's calling the Spirit 'unbegotten' means only 'not begotten,' as his division of beings shows (c4).
claims: The Holy Spirit is not born and is not a son.
If the Spirit were begotten of both, he would be son of both, which is absurd.
The Son proceeds by birth, the Spirit as gift.
Generation and procession cannot be distinguished by us in this life; both are ineffable.
The Spirit is neither begotten nor unbegotten.
'Unbegotten' in the proper sense belongs to the Father alone.

pl-l1d14.summary: Distinguishes the Spirit's eternal procession from his temporal procession, his mission or giving to sanctify creatures. In both he proceeds jointly from Father and Son. Bede identifies the temporal procession with the giving of grace, and Augustine sees it in Christ's breathing on the disciples and in the two givings, on earth for love of neighbor and from heaven for love of God (c1). Against those who say only the Spirit's gifts are given, Lombard holds with Augustine and Ambrose that the Spirit himself, God, is given and poured into minds: only God gives God, and the Spirit, undivided and present to many at once, gives a gift equal to himself without being lessened by being sent (c2). Holy men, even apostles, do not and cannot give the Spirit: they pray for him, Christ gave him as God, and Paul 'gave' him only as minister of preaching (c3).
claims: The Spirit has an eternal and a temporal procession, both from Father and Son jointly.
The temporal procession is the giving or mission of the Spirit to sanctify creatures.
The Spirit himself, not only his gifts, is given to humans.
Being sent or given does not make the Spirit lesser.
No human, however holy, can give the Spirit; ministers only pray and preach.

pl-l1d15.summary: Treats the missions. The Spirit gives himself as God and is given as Gift, so, since giving is a common work of the three, he is sent and proceeds temporally also from himself. Son and Spirit are sent where they already were (c1). The Son's mission is the incarnation, his being made of a woman, done by Father, Spirit, and the Son himself as an inseparable work, without change of place or of the Word (c2–4). 'I have not come of myself' is said of his humanity (c5). Besides the eternal generation, better called begetting, the Son is sent in two ways: once, visibly, to be man, and often, invisibly, to holy souls and angels, to be with man and be known, which is not a sending 'into the world' (c6–8). The Father is never sent, because he has the authority of principle as the source of the whole deity (c9), and sending implies no inequality, only that authority (c10).
claims: The Spirit is given and sent by Father, Son, and himself, since mission is a common divine work.
Son and Spirit are sent where they already were.
The Son's visible mission is the incarnation, a work of the whole Trinity.
The Son was sent visibly once, and is sent invisibly often to holy souls.
The Father is never sent, because he is the principle of the whole deity.
Being sent does not imply inequality.

pl-l1d16.summary: Treats the Spirit's visible mission. Like the Son, the Spirit is sent visibly (the dove; wind and tongues of fire at Pentecost) and invisibly into minds. With Augustine, the visible signs were creatures made in time to turn hearts to the eternal, signifying the inner infusion without showing his substance or any local motion. The Son is called less than the Father according to his mission because he assumed humanity into personal union, while the Spirit did not become a dove (c1). As man the Son is less than the Father, the Spirit, and himself, equal by nature and less by habitus. Hilary's view that the Father is greater by the authority of giving, without the Son being less, is to be read piously (c2).
claims: The Spirit was sent visibly through creaturely signs that signified his invisible infusion.
The Spirit's substance was not seen and he did not move locally.
The Son is less than the Father insofar as he became man.
The Spirit is not called less because he did not assume a creature into personal union.
As man the Son is less than the Father, the Spirit, and himself.
The Father is 'greater' by authority of origin, without the Son being less in nature.

pl-l1d17.summary: Gives Lombard's distinctive thesis on the Spirit's invisible mission: the Spirit himself is the charity by which we love God and neighbor, and he is sent when he makes us love. With Augustine, the love by which we love the brother is God, better known than the brother (c1); that love is the Holy Spirit, the greatest gift (c2); 'God is charity' is said essentially, not causally like 'God is my patience' (c3). Charity, the most excellent gift, alone divides the saved from the lost, and through it the whole Trinity dwells in us (c4). Charity grows in us without the Spirit changing: properly, we advance in him; he is everywhere but not had by all; and he was given to Christ without measure (c5). Against objections, Lombard holds that God's charity and ours are one, named for different reasons. Charity is from the Spirit because he gives himself, unlike faith, which is only a gift. It is called a motion of the mind because it moves the mind. The Spirit produces acts of faith and hope through those virtues but the act of love immediately (c6).
claims: The Holy Spirit is the charity by which we love God and neighbor.
The Spirit is sent invisibly when he makes us love God and neighbor.
'God is charity' is an essential, not a causal, predication.
Charity is the most excellent gift, without which no other gift leads to God.
Charity grows in us while the Spirit remains unchangeable; properly, we advance in him.
God's charity and ours are one and the same, named for different reasons.
The Spirit works the act of love directly, without a created virtue mediating, but acts of faith and hope through those virtues.

pl-l1d18.summary: Treats the Spirit as Gift. Through the Gift that is the Spirit, proper gifts are divided to each, while all the good have the Gift in common (c1). 'Given' applies to him only in time, but 'Gift' eternally, because he eternally proceeds from Father and Son as giftable to creatures. For the Spirit, being Gift is proceeding, as for the Son being born is being from the Father, and 'Holy Spirit' and 'Gift' are relative names (c2). By proceeding the Spirit receives not only to be Gift but to be the divine essence, as the Son does by birth, though neither is essence by his personal property (c3). As eternal Gift he is referred to Father and Son, as given also to recipients, so he is called 'our' spirit, the one received to make us holy (c4). The Son is 'our bread' but not 'our Son,' and Scripture never says 'our Holy Spirit' (c5). Whether the Spirit is referred to himself is deferred (c6).
claims: Gifts are divided through the Gift, the Holy Spirit, whom all the good have in common.
The Spirit is eternally Gift and temporally given.
For the Spirit, being Gift is proceeding from Father and Son.
By procession the Spirit receives the whole divine essence, as the Son does by birth.
The given Spirit is referred to giver and recipients and called 'ours.'
'Son' and 'Holy Spirit' are relative only to the divine persons.

pl-l1d19.summary: Treats the coequality of the three persons: none exceeds another in eternity, magnitude, or power (c1), which are one divine essence (c2). In magnitude no person is greater, nor two than one, since the whole essence is in each (c3). Hence the persons are in one another, by the fullness of divinity and unity of nature, as Augustine, Hilary, and Ambrose agree, though we see it only in a mirror (c4). No person is a part of God (c5–6). Essence is not predicated of the persons as genus of species or species of individuals (c7), nor as common matter like the gold of three statues (c8), nor as a common nature like that of three men (c9). Lombard reconciles John Damascene's language of universal substance and particular hypostases by reading it as analogy, holding that Augustine's teaching must be kept (c9). The persons differ in number only in being counted, and are better said to be distinguished by properties (c10). Magnitude is truth, and no person is truer than another (c11). So God is triune but not triple (c12).
claims: The three persons are coequal in eternity, magnitude, and power, which are one essence.
The whole divine essence is in each person.
The persons are in one another by unity of nature.
No person is a part of God, and several persons are not greater than one.
Essence is not predicated of the persons as genus, species, matter, or common nature.
Damascene's universal–particular language is to be read by analogy; Augustine prevails.
The persons are distinguished by properties, not as numerically distinct individuals.
God is triune, not triple.

pl-l1d20.summary: Completes the treatment of equality with power. No person is more powerful than another, since the Son received the Father's omnipotence by birth and the Spirit by procession (c1). Following Augustine against Maximinus: 'All that the Father has is mine' implies equal power (c2). A Father who begot a lesser Son would be either weak or envious, and a human father would beget an equal if he could. Origin (who is from whom) and equality (how great) are different questions, since generation implies an order of nature, not inequality. So no person exceeds another in eternity, magnitude, or power (c3).
claims: The three persons have one and equal power.
The Son received omnipotence by birth, the Spirit by procession.
All that the Father has belongs to the Son, including omnipotence.
A Father who begot a lesser Son would be weak or envious.
Origin and equality are distinct questions; generation implies order, not inequality.

pl-l1d21.summary: Treats exclusive terms (solus) in Trinitarian speech. 'The Father alone' does not separate him from the inseparable Son and Spirit but excludes them from his property: only the Father is Father, only the Son Son, only the Spirit Holy Spirit (c1). The Trinity together is properly 'the only God'; 'only the Father is God' should not be said in our own words, and scriptural texts on the 'only' God, against Maximinus, refer to the Trinity (c2). The Trinity is 'God alone' though always with saints, because nothing else is God; what is said of one person does not exclude the others, and where Father and Son are named, the Spirit, their peace, is understood (c3).
claims: 'Alone' with a personal name excludes others from the personal property, not from the person's company.
The Trinity is properly the only God.
'Only the Father is God' should not be said except following authority.
Scriptural 'only God' texts refer to the Trinity, not the Father alone.
What is said of one person does not exclude the inseparable others.

pl-l1d22.summary: Begins the treatise on divine names. With Augustine and Ambrose, some names are proper to single persons (Son, Word), some signify the unity of essence and are said of each and all (wisdom, power), and some are metaphorical (splendor, mirror) (c1). Some names apply from time relatively to creatures, either to all persons (Lord, Creator) or not (given, sent) (c2); 'Trinity' is a quasi-collective name of all three together, and some temporal names are non-relative ('incarnate'), giving six kinds (c3). Personal names are said relatively; essential names are said 'ad se,' substantially, and singularly in sum: each is God, great, and omnipotent, but not three gods; God is great not by participation but by being his own magnitude (c4).
claims: Divine names are personal, essential, or metaphorical.
Some names are temporal and relative to creatures; some temporal names are non-relative.
'Trinity' is a quasi-collective name said only of the three together.
Personal names are relative; essential names are substantial and singular in sum.
God is great by being his own magnitude, not by participation.

pl-l1d23.summary: Treats 'person.' Unlike other substantial names, 'person' is said of each according to substance yet plurally in sum, 'three persons,' from the poverty of language, so as not to be silent when asked 'three what?' (c1). Greeks say one ousia, three hypostases; Latins one essence, three persons; God is thought more truly than spoken, and is more truly than thought (c2). We say three persons but not three gods because Scripture forbids the latter (Deut 6:4) (c3), and not three essences lest diversity be implied, while denying three would be Sabellian (c4). In God there is neither diversity nor singularity or solitude: God is one but not singular; the persons are distinct but not separated; 'diverse persons' means distinct (c5). Likewise there is no multiplicity: God is triune and simple, not multiple (c6).
claims: 'Person' is said substantially of each yet plurally of the three.
'Three persons' is said by necessity of speech, not to express the ineffable.
Greek 'hypostasis' corresponds to Latin 'person.'
We say three persons, not three gods or essences.
God is one but not singular; the persons are distinct but not diverse or separated.
God is triune and simple, not multiple.

pl-l1d24.summary: Asks what number words signify in God. Lombard holds, following the authorities, that they were introduced to exclude rather than to posit: 'one God' excludes many gods; 'several persons' excludes singularity and solitude (Hilary on 'let us make'); 'three persons' means Father, Son, and Spirit and no other, with no numerical quantity; 'distinct' excludes Sabellian confusion without positing diversity; 'Trinity' signifies what 'three persons' does, so no person is the Trinity. Isidore's 'singular' and 'multiple' are read as 'one' and 'triune' (c1).
claims: Number words in God exclude rather than posit.
'One God' excludes many gods; 'several persons' excludes solitude.
'Three persons' posits no numerical quantity.
'Distinct' excludes confusion, not unity.
No single person is the Trinity.

pl-l1d25.summary: Determines the meaning of 'person.' If in 'three persons' it meant essence, there would be three essences; some still argue it signifies essence there, but this cannot explain 'other personally' (c1). Lombard's account: 'person' has several meanings, judged from the reasons for speaking (Hilary). Properly it signifies essence; in 'three persons' it signifies subsistences, Greek hypostases; 'three what?' asked what three things the faith confesses, and the three things are one supreme thing (c2). 'Other person' means other subsistence; 'other personally' means other by personal property (paternity, filiation, procession). So 'person' has three senses: essence, hypostasis, and property, as Jerome and Damascene confirm (c3).
claims: 'Person' is equivocal, to be read from the reasons for speaking.
Properly 'person' signifies essence.
In 'three persons' it signifies subsistences or hypostases.
'Other personally' means other by personal property.
'Person' signifies essence, hypostasis, or property depending on use.

pl-l1d26.summary: Treats the personal properties. Jerome's warning that poison lies under 'hypostasis' targets heretical misuse, not the term (c1). The properties, also called notions or relations, are begetting, being born, and proceeding (paternity, filiation, procession), designated by the relative names; they are eternally and immutably in the persons, not accidental (c2). With Augustine, things are said of God by substance or by relation, never by accident (c3). The Son is Son by property of origin and truth of birth, while humans are sons by adoption and grace, sons of the whole Trinity, which is called Father only metaphorically (c4–5). The Spirit is Gift by an eternal property; 'Gift' and 'Holy Spirit' express the same relation; he bears as proper the name common to Father and Son (c6). The Trinity can be called holy spirit only essentially (c7). Not all relatives have reciprocal names: 'Spirit of the Father' but not 'Father of the Spirit'; 'gift of the giver' and 'giver of the gift' (c8).
claims: The personal properties are paternity, filiation, and procession.
Divine relations are eternal and immutable, not accidents.
Nothing is said of God by accident; things are said by substance or relation.
The Son is Son by nature; humans are sons by adoption, sons of the whole Trinity.
The Spirit is Gift by eternal property and bears a name common to Father and Son.
Not all relative terms have reciprocal correlatives.

pl-l1d27.summary: Identifies Hilary's properties (always Father, always Son) with Augustine's (begetting, being begotten, proceeding) and with paternity, filiation, procession (c1). Yet personal names signify both a relation and a hypostasis, while relational terms signify only relations; in 'God begot,' 'God' stands for the hypostasis (c2). The properties determine and distinguish the persons without separating them (Damascene); begetter, begotten, Word, and Image are also relative personal names, the Son being Word and Image by the same notion by which he is Son, while wisdom is essential (c3). What is said 'ad se' of Father and Son is said of both together (c4). Essential names can stand for persons, as 'God from God' for the Son alone or 'God died'; 'this from that' is said only with essential names; 'God' can also stand for the whole Trinity (c5).
claims: Hilary and Augustine name the same personal properties.
Personal names signify a hypostasis with its relation.
Properties distinguish the persons without separating them.
Word and Image are relative names of the Son; wisdom is essential.
Essential names can stand for persons or for the whole Trinity.

pl-l1d28.summary: Treats further notions. 'Unbegotten' is relative, said only of the Father, a notion distinct from paternity (innascibility); it means 'not-begotten,' and a negation does not make a relative term substantial (c1). Opinions differ whether the Spirit may be called 'not-begotten' (c2). Hilary names the Father's property innascibility (c3). Against the Arian argument from 'unbegotten' and 'begotten,' Ambrose notes that 'unbegotten' is unscriptural; some true terms may be passed over in silence because of heretics (c4). Being Father and being Son differ by notion, but the Father's being and the Son's being are the same essence (c5). 'Begotten Wisdom' is the Son, with 'wisdom' standing for the hypostasis, so the essence is not begotten (c6). 'Image' is sometimes said substantially, of the Trinity to which man is made (c7).
claims: 'Unbegotten' is a relative notion proper to the Father, distinct from paternity.
A negated relative term remains relative.
Some true expressions may prudently be omitted because of heretics.
Being Father and being Son differ by notion, not by essence.
In 'begotten Wisdom,' 'wisdom' stands for the hypostasis.
'Image' can also signify the essence of the Trinity.

pl-l1d29.summary: Treats 'principle.' The Father is principle of the whole deity, being from no one; the Son is principle of the Spirit; the Spirit is principle only of creatures; the Father is principle without principle, the Son principle from principle, the Spirit principle from both (c1). Eternally the Father is principle of the Son and Father and Son of the Spirit; temporally the Trinity began to be one principle of creatures, not three, as one creator, since they work in the same way; all natures are from God, not sins (c2). The Father is principle and author of the Son by generation; the Son is from the unbeginning Father but does not have a beginning (c3). Father and Son are principle of the Spirit by one unnamed notion, neither paternity nor filiation; 'giver' is temporal (c4).
claims: The Father is principle of the whole deity because he is from none.
The Trinity is one principle of creatures, as one creator.
The Trinity began to be principle of creatures in time.
The Father is author of the Son by generation.
Father and Son are one principle of the Spirit by one unnamed notion.

pl-l1d30.summary: Treats names said of God from time and relatively to creatures: Creator, Lord, refuge, given. With Augustine, God is not lord eternally since creatures are not eternal; he began to be lord even of time. Such names are said by an accident of the creature, not of God: as a coin becomes 'price' without change, God becomes our refuge or Father by our change. The relation is in the creature, not the Creator (c1). This resolves whether the Spirit, giving himself, is related to himself: 'given' relates him to giver and recipient, and the change is in the recipient (c2).
claims: Temporal relative names apply to God without change in him.
God is not eternally lord, since creatures are not eternal.
Such names are said by accident of the creature, not of God.
The relation of creature to Creator is in the creature only.
The Spirit as given is related to giver and recipient, not to himself.

pl-l1d31.summary: Treats equality and the appropriated triads. 'Equal' and 'similar' are relative names, yet the persons are equal by substance, so equality is non-disparity, not a relation; it may be read as removing inequality (c1). Hilary's 'eternity in the Father, form in the Image, use in the Gift,' explained by Augustine, marks the Father as from no one, the Son as perfect image and art of God, the Spirit as delight of Father and Son; Lombard finds it very difficult. Augustine's 'unity in the Father, equality in the Son, concord in the Spirit' likewise shows the distinction of persons (c2). Unity is attributed to the Father because he is from none and all from him are one with him (c3). The three are 'one thing' and one God, not 'one person'; 'one' in John 10:30 refutes Arius and 'are' refutes Sabellius (c4). Equality is attributed to the Son, tentatively, because he is begotten equal (c5), and connection to the Spirit as the love and communion of Father and Son (c6).
claims: 'Equal' is a relative name, but the persons are equal by substance.
Hilary's eternity, form, and use are appropriated to Father, Son, and Spirit.
Augustine's unity, equality, and concord are appropriated to Father, Son, and Spirit.
The three are one thing and one God, not one person.
John 10:30 refutes both Arius and Sabellius.
The Spirit is the connection and concord of Father and Son.

pl-l1d32.summary: Treats whether the persons love and are wise by the persons proceeding from them. With Augustine, Father and Son love and keep unity by their essence and their own Gift, but the Father does not love only through the Spirit (c1). The Father is not wise by the wisdom he begot, since in God to be is to be wise; Augustine's earlier contrary statement was retracted. The Father is unbegotten wisdom, the Son begotten wisdom, yet one wisdom (c2). The Son is wise through himself but not from himself (c3). Arguments for two wisdoms in the Father are sophistical (c4). As the Spirit is love that is the Trinity without being the Trinity, the Son is wisdom that is the Trinity without being it (c5). Lombard confesses he cannot reconcile the parity between not being wise by begotten wisdom and loving by the proceeding love; he excludes the error that Father and Son are by the Spirit and leaves the question to readers (c6).
claims: Father and Son love by their essence and their Gift, not only by the Spirit.
The Father is not wise by the wisdom he begot.
Father and Son are one wisdom: unbegotten and begotten.
The Son is wise through himself but not from himself.
The relation between the Father's loving and the Spirit as love is left an open question.

pl-l1d33.summary: Asks whether the personal properties are the persons and the divine essence. Lombard affirms that they are in the persons and are the persons and the essence, since in God the haver is what is had (Jerome, Hilary), rejecting the view that they are affixed externally. Since properties determine hypostases, not nature (Damascene), the essence neither begets nor is begotten, avoiding Sabellianism (c1). How they can be in the essence without determining it exceeds understanding (Hilary). Augustine's texts on Ps 68 and on the Word are read as saying the Father is not Father by the essence, without denying that the property is the essence (c2).
claims: The personal properties are the persons and the divine essence.
The view that properties are extrinsically affixed is rejected.
Properties determine hypostases, not the nature.
The essence neither begets nor is begotten.
How properties are in the essence without determining it is incomprehensible.

pl-l1d34.summary: Refutes those who separate the divine nature from the persons, citing Hilary's 'nature is not the same as thing of nature': Hilary refers to creatures, and in God the persons are the same nature; there is a rational distinction of essence and hypostasis, but the persons are one by essence and differ by properties (c1). One says 'one essence of three persons,' not 'one God of three persons,' which would imply creaturely subjection (c2). Power, wisdom, and goodness are one in the three, yet appropriated to Father, Son, and Spirit (c3), so that we do not measure God by creatures, as if the Father were weakened by age, the Son immature, or the Spirit harsh (Hugh of St Victor) (c4). Homoousion, defended at Nicaea and vindicated after Rimini, expresses 'I and the Father are one'; metaphorical names are to be read from their likeness; the treatise on the Trinity ends confessing its ineffability (c5).
claims: The divine nature is the same as the persons.
Hilary's distinction of nature and thing of nature applies to creatures.
Essence and hypostasis differ by reason, not in reality.
Power, wisdom, and goodness are one but appropriated to the persons.
Appropriation prevents measuring God by creatures.
Homoousion expresses the unity of Father and Son.

pl-l1d35.summary: Begins the treatment of special attributes: knowledge, foreknowledge, providence, disposition, predestination, will, and power. God's one simple knowledge takes many names by its objects (c1): foreknowledge of all future things, good and evil (c2); disposition of things to be made (c3); predestination of those to be saved and the goods prepared for them, by eternal election (c4); providence of things to be governed (c5); knowledge of all things, temporal and eternal, God alone knowing himself perfectly (c6). If nothing were future, God would not be called foreknowing, but his knowledge would be the same, since these names are relative to objects yet signify essence (c7–8). All things are in God from eternity as in his knowledge, which is life, not in his essence; to him all are present (c9).
claims: God's knowledge is one and simple but named variously by its objects.
Foreknowledge concerns all future things, good and evil.
Predestination is God's eternal election of the saved and preparation of goods for them.
Names like foreknowledge are relative to objects but signify essence.
God's knowledge would be the same if nothing were future.
All things are in God's knowledge from eternity and present to him.

pl-l1d36.summary: Asks in what sense things are in God. Things in God's knowledge or presence are not in his essence; he has the elect before creation in his presence, not in his nature (c1). Though God knows good and evil, evils are not in God: he knows goods by knowledge and approval, evils only by knowledge; 'I do not know you' means disapproval; what is in him is what he authors (c2). 'From him, through him, in him' mean the same, and since God authors only goods, only goods are in him; sins arise from the will (c3). These prepositions are appropriated to the persons but apply to each (c4). What is 'from God' (creation) is not 'of God' (his substance), as a house is from its builder but of wood (c5).
claims: Things in God's knowledge are not in his essence.
God has the elect in his presence before they exist.
Evils are not in God; God knows them but does not approve or author them.
Only goods are in God, since he is their author.
'From,' 'through,' and 'in him' are appropriated but apply to each person.
Creatures are from God, but not of his substance.

pl-l1d37.summary: Lombard's treatment of the ways God is in things, arising as a digression from the discussion of divine knowledge and whether things are 'in God'. He establishes that God is everywhere by essence, presence, and power, yet dwells only in the good by grace (c1-3), defends divine purity against contamination by things (c4), and then argues that God is neither local nor temporal and changes by neither place nor time (c5-9). To this end he distinguishes bodily locality (dimension plus place-definition) from created spirits' locality (place-definition only) and from God's complete non-locality, answering the objection that God's coming to be in new creatures implies change.
claims: God is essentially, presentially, and potentially in all things without limitation or change.
God dwells by grace only in the good, and in Christ by the grace of union.
God's presence to things does not defile him (simplicity and purity).
God is neither circumscribed nor moved by place or time; created spirits are local in a qualified sense, bodies wholly so.
God's beginning to be in new creatures implies no change in God.
The mode of God's essential omnipresence exceeds human comprehension.

pl-l1d38.summary: Asks whether God's knowledge or foreknowledge causes things or things cause it. Foreknowledge seems to impose necessity, and Augustine says things are because God knows them; but then God would cause evils, and things cannot cause the eternal's knowledge. Reconciling Augustine with Origen ('things are foreknown because they will be'), Lombard holds that future things do not cause God's knowledge, and his knowledge as mere knowing is only a cause 'without which not,' while knowledge with good pleasure and disposition causes what he does. Evils he foreknows by knowledge alone, without causing them, as the Jews' unbelief (c1). Against the objection that foreknowledge could be deceived, he distinguishes the conjoined sense (true: what is foreknown cannot fail to happen) from the disjoined (false: this event could not have happened otherwise) (c2).
claims: God's foreknowledge does not of itself cause things or impose necessity.
Future things do not cause God's knowledge.
God's knowledge with good pleasure causes what he does; mere knowledge is a condition only.
God foreknows evils without causing them.
Foreknowledge cannot be deceived, yet events remain contingent.
Modal statements about foreknowledge are true conjointly and false disjointly.

pl-l1d39.summary: Asks whether God's knowledge can increase or decrease. It cannot: his knowledge is his essence, and the Son knows all as he receives being; all things are seen at once. Yet God can know what he does not know, since objects could differ without change in knowledge (c1). He cannot know anything newly in time, nor will anything newly, though he can will what he never willed (c2). He could know more things if he made more, without his knowledge growing (c3). Against Jerome's denial that God knows the number of gnats moment by moment, Lombard reads Jerome as denying successive knowledge and equal providence for irrational creatures: God has general providence for all and special providence for rational creatures (c4).
claims: God's knowledge is immutable, being his essence.
God knows all things simultaneously.
God can know what he does not know only by variation in objects.
God cannot know or will anything newly.
God has general providence for all creatures and special providence for rational ones.

pl-l1d40.summary: Treats predestination and reprobation. Predestination is the preparation of grace, presupposing foreknowledge; God predestined the elect and reprobated others, foreknowing their sins; the number of the elect is fixed. 'The predestined cannot be damned' is true conjointly and false disjointly, since God could from eternity not have predestined him; possibility here refers to God's unchanging power (c1). Reprobation is foreknowledge of unrepented iniquity and preparation of punishment: God foreknows sin but prepares only punishment. Hardening, the effect of reprobation, is not imparting malice but withholding grace, by a hidden equity at which Paul marvels (c2).
claims: Predestination is the preparation of grace and presupposes foreknowledge.
The number of the elect is fixed.
The predestined cannot be damned in the conjoined sense, but could have been in the disjoined sense.
Reprobation is foreknowledge of iniquity and preparation of punishment, not of sin.
Hardening is the withholding of grace, not the imparting of malice.
God's withholding of grace rests on hidden equity.

pl-l1d41.summary: Holds that mercy has no merit (lest grace be emptied), while hardening is rendered by judgment for merits; neither predestination nor reprobation has merits, as with Jacob and Esau (c1). Lombard rejects election on foreseen faith, which Augustine retracted since faith too is God's gift: God chose so that people would be good, not because they would be. He suggests Augustine's 'most hidden merits' was likewise retracted, rejects as frivolous the idea that some merit not being refused grace, and rejects the preexistence of souls; faithful ignorance is better than rash knowledge. Reprobation does not cause evil as predestination causes good (c2). God ceases to foreknow things once they are no longer future but always knows what he once knew; the same knowledge is expressed in different tenses, as the patriarchs' faith and ours are one (c3).
claims: Mercy has no merit; hardening is by judgment.
Predestination and reprobation are not based on merits, present or foreseen.
Election is not based on foreseen faith; faith is God's gift.
God elects so that people become good.
Preexistence of souls is rejected.
Reprobation does not cause evil.
God always knows what he once knew; tenses change, not knowledge.

pl-l1d42.summary: Treats omnipotence. God can do all things, though he does only what befits his truth and justice (c1). Walking and speaking belong to his power since he works them in creatures; he cannot sin, lie, die, or be deceived, which shows power, not impotence (c2). With Hugh, God does all he wills and suffers nothing. Augustine's 'omnipotent because he can do whatever he wills' excludes evils and answers those who limited God's power; unlike saints, God can do all he wills to be done. The Son and Spirit act through themselves, not from themselves, by natural power from the Father, whereas creatures have gratuitous power (c3).
claims: God can do all things that befit him.
Inability to sin, lie, or suffer is not impotence.
God does all he wills and suffers nothing.
God can do whatever he wills to be done, directly or through creatures.
The Son and Spirit have the same natural power from the Father.

pl-l1d43.summary: Refutes those who limit God's power, holding he cannot do otherwise, better, or omit what he does. Each argument is answered by distinguishing senses: God can do only what would be good if done, but much that never will be; 'exacts' and 'ought' are improper of God, who is debtor only by promise; he could act otherwise by the same eternal reason; the foreknowledge argument is answered by the earlier distinction. Authorities that God cannot do what he does not will, or that his power is not greater than his will, mean that power and will are one, not that more things are subject to his will than his power. Scripture and Augustine show God can do much he does not will (twelve legions, Judas's conversion, justifying all), and can will what he never willed, though not newly (c1).
claims: God can do other than he does and omit what he does.
God can do only what would be good if done, but much that never will be.
'Ought' and 'exacts' are not properly said of God.
God's power and will are one, but more things are subject to his power than his will.
God can will what he never willed, but not by a new will.

pl-l1d44.summary: Asks whether God can make things better than he does. The argument from the begetting of an equal Son fails, since creatures are not from God's substance. If creation were supremely good it would equal God; its inability to receive more good is a defect God can remedy; he could have made man unable to sin. God cannot act with greater wisdom, but can give creatures better modes of being; another mode of redemption was possible, though none more fitting (c1). God always can do whatever he once could: the power to be incarnate and to have been incarnate is the same power, as with knowledge and will across tenses (c2).
claims: God can make things better than he does.
Creation cannot be supremely good without equaling God.
God cannot act with greater wisdom, but can give creatures a better mode of being.
Another mode of redemption was possible, though none more fitting.
God always has every power he ever had.

pl-l1d45.summary: Treats God's will. Will is said of God by essence: to will is to be, and it is not an affection (c1), though God is not all he wills, as he knows all without being all (c2); objects added to 'wills' or 'knows' signify what is subject to the essence (c3). God's supremely good will is the uncaused first cause of all forms, motions, and events, whose cause must not be sought; God made heaven and earth because he willed (c4). Properly, God's will is his one immutable good pleasure (c5). Figuratively, precept, prohibition, counsel, permission, and operation are called his will as signs of it, as signs of anger are called anger (c6). God does not will all he commands (Abraham); he permits evils and does goods; his good pleasure is always fulfilled, its signs often not (c7).
claims: God's will is his essence, not an affection.
God's will is the uncaused first cause of all things.
The cause of God's will is not to be sought.
Properly, God's will is his one immutable good pleasure.
Precept, prohibition, counsel, permission, and operation are called God's will as its signs.
God's good pleasure is always fulfilled; its signs often are not.

pl-l1d46.summary: Asks how God's will is always fulfilled if he 'wills all men to be saved' and willed to gather Jerusalem's children. With Augustine, he gathered all he willed despite Jerusalem's refusal, and 1 Tim 2:4 means no one is saved unless God wills it; the Omnipotent never willed what was not done (c1–2). Do evils happen by God's will? Some say God wills evils to happen, since otherwise he would be impotent and since it is good that evils exist; others that he neither wills nor nills them but only does not will them, being permitter, not author (c3). 'It is good that evils happen' means God draws good from them for the elect (Rom 8:28), not that evil is simply good (c4–5); evils borne patiently profit the faithful, but God makes no one worse, and man becomes worse by vice of will (c6). God causes being, not defect; the sophism that the truth of 'evils happen' is from God fails. Siding with the sounder view, God does not will evils to happen, nor wills them not to happen; many things happen that he does not will (c7).
claims: God's will is never frustrated.
'God wills all to be saved' means no one is saved unless God wills it.
God does not will evils to happen, nor wills them not to happen.
God is permitter, not author, of evils.
'It is good that evils happen' means God draws good from them.
Man becomes worse by his own vice of will, not by God.
God causes being, not defect.

pl-l1d47.summary: Holds that God's will is always effective and fulfilled concerning man however he turns: by us when we do good, concerning us when we sin; God fulfills his will even through sinful wills, using evils for the damnation of some and the salvation of others. 'Against God's will' refers to the signs of his will (c1). Many things are done against his precept but not apart from his permission; sinners fulfill his eternal will by resisting his precept (Gregory); his will is unconquered and never unjust (c2). God's eternal will is always fulfilled, while his precepts are not; he commands all to show his justice and leave the wicked without excuse, willing some, not all, to obey (c3).
claims: God's will is always effective; nothing in free will overcomes it.
God's will is fulfilled by us or concerning us.
Evils are done against God's precept but not apart from his permission.
Sinners fulfill God's eternal will by resisting his precept.
God's precepts show his justice and leave the wicked inexcusable.

pl-l1d48.summary: Concludes Book 1 on the conformity of human and divine wills. A human will can be evil while willing what God wills and good while willing otherwise; its goodness depends on what befits a human to will and its end (c1). God's good will is fulfilled through evil wills, as in the crucifixion: God willed Christ's passion, not the Jews' act, which he neither willed nor nilled; Christ's death was so good that Peter was rebuked for opposing it (c2). The saints should be pleased by Christ's passion for redemption, not for his suffering (c3). Only Christ's passion redeems; the saints' passions may be willed or not with good will according to right ends, as with Paul (c4).
claims: A will's goodness depends on what befits one to will and its end, not only on agreement with God's will.
God fulfills his good will through evil human wills.
God willed Christ's passion but not the Jews' sin.
One may rejoice and grieve over the same event for different reasons.
Only Christ's passion redeems; the saints' passions may be willed or not, rightly.

pl-l2d1.summary: Opens Book 2 on creation. Gen 1:1 shows God as the one creator and principle of all, against Plato's three uncreated principles; to create is to make from nothing (c1), which belongs to God alone, while creatures make from matter (c2). God makes without motion or change, by a new effect of his eternal will, against Aristotle's eternal world; the only cause of creation is God's goodness, freely sharing his beatitude (c3). God made rational creatures, angels and humans, to understand, love, possess, and enjoy him, for their benefit, not his; man was made for God and the world for man, so man stands in the middle, serving and served (c4). Man was not made only to restore the fallen angels (c5). The soul was joined to the body because God willed it and as an example of the future union of the rational spirit with God; man is made of a body from earth and a soul from nothing. The treatise will consider angels first, then corporeal creatures (c6).
claims: God is the one creator and principle; to create is to make from nothing.
God creates without change, by a new effect of his eternal will.
The world is not eternal.
God's goodness is the sole cause of creation, freely sharing his beatitude.
Rational creatures were made to know, love, and enjoy God, for their benefit.
Man was made for God, and the world for man.
The union of soul and body exemplifies the future union of the spirit with God.

pl-l2d2.summary: Treats when and where angels were created. Against texts implying angels were made before all else, Lombard holds that spiritual and corporeal creation were made simultaneously, angels first in dignity, not time (c1), with time itself, not in time (c2); Jerome's view that angels served God for ages before the world is likely a report of others' opinion (c3). The angels were created in the empyrean heaven, above the firmament, from which some fell (c4). Both the matter of visible things and the angelic nature were created partly unformed: matter as confused chaos, angels lacking the form they would receive by conversion to their Creator (c5). Lucifer's 'I will ascend into heaven' (Isa 14:13) does not imply he was not already in the empyrean: 'heaven' there means equality with God (c6).
claims: Spiritual and corporeal creation were made simultaneously, with time.
Angels are prior to bodies in dignity, not time.
The angels were created in the empyrean heaven.
Unformed matter and angelic nature were created together, each partly unformed.
Angels receive their full form by love and conversion to God.
Lucifer's 'ascending into heaven' means seeking equality with God.

pl-l2d3.summary: Treats the angels' condition at creation. They were given simple, immaterial essence, personal distinctness, intellect, memory, and will, and free choice to turn to good or evil without coercion (c1). They differed in subtlety of nature, perspicacity of wisdom, and aptitude of choice, and those higher by nature later received greater grace and rank (Hugh) (c2), while all equally are spirits, indissoluble, and immortal (c3). Against the view that the fallen angels were created evil and fell at once, Lombard holds with Augustine that all were created good, innocent but not yet just, falling after a brief interval from the good they would have received; Job 40:19 refers to God's use of the devil, not his created nature (c4). Before fall or confirmation, angels had natural knowledge of themselves, their maker, and their fellows, and of good and evil (c5), and a natural, non-meritorious love of God and themselves (c6).
claims: Angels have simple immaterial essence, intellect and will, and free choice.
Angels were unequal in natural gifts, and grace followed nature.
All angels were created good, innocent but not yet just.
The fallen angels fell by their own will after a brief interval.
Before confirmation angels had natural knowledge and natural, non-meritorious love.

pl-l2d4.summary: Asks whether angels were created blessed or miserable, perfect or imperfect. They were created neither blessed nor miserable: misery comes only from sin, and the fallen did not foreknow their fall. Augustine's suggestion that the good foreknew their beatitude was conjectural, and Lombard thinks it more probable that none were blessed before confirmation, unless innocence is called beatitude. Perfection is threefold: by time (angels at creation), by nature (angels after confirmation, saints after resurrection), and universal (God alone) (c1).
claims: Angels were created neither blessed nor miserable.
Misery comes only from sin.
No angel was blessed before confirmation, most probably.
Perfection is by time, by nature, or universal; universal perfection is God's alone.

pl-l2d5.summary: Treats the division of angels by conversion and aversion. Some turned to God by charity and were illumined by grace; others turned away in envy born of pride and were blinded by the absence of grace, not by infused malice; both acts were free (c1). Angels were created able to will either way, and God divided light from darkness, good angels from bad (c2). The converted received cooperating grace, without which the creature cannot advance to merit, though it can fall by itself (c3); not justifying grace, since they were not evil, but grace to love God perfectly and persevere (c4). The fallen are to blame: they could have stood by their created gifts until grace was added, and fell by their own will (c5). The good angels were blessed at confirmation; Lombard prefers the view that they did not merit that beatitude but merit it afterward by ministering to us, so reward preceded merit (c6).
claims: Some angels turned to God by charity, others away by pride and envy.
Conversion and aversion were free acts.
The converted angels received cooperating grace.
The creature can fall by itself but cannot advance to merit without grace.
The fallen angels fell by their own fault, being able to stand.
The good angels were blessed at confirmation and merit afterward by their ministry.

pl-l2d6.summary: Treats the fall and the demons. Angels of every rank both fell and stood; the chief of the fallen, Lucifer, was the most excellent of all, and in pride wished to equal God in power (c1). He was cast from the empyrean into the dark air with his accomplices, for our testing (c2); the air is their prison until judgment, when they will be cast into hell (c3). Demons have a hierarchy and rule over provinces, persons, or vices, and the devil uses riches to tempt (c4). Some demons likely lead souls to hell and torment them there (c5). Lucifer may be bound in hell and will be loosed at the time of Antichrist, when he will be given power to tempt (c6). Demons defeated by chaste saints may lose the power to tempt others, perhaps only in the vice in which they were defeated (Origen) (c7).
claims: Lucifer, the most excellent angel, fell by pride, wishing to equal God.
The fallen angels dwell in the dark air until judgment, for our testing.
Demons have hierarchy and specialize in tempting to particular vices.
Some demons lead souls to hell and torment them.
Lucifer will be given power to tempt under Antichrist.
Saints who defeat demons diminish their power.

pl-l2d7.summary: Treats the state of good and bad angels after the fall. The good are confirmed so they cannot sin; the bad so obstinate they cannot will well (c1). Both keep free choice, since both act by their own will without coercion; the bad have it but corrupted (c2). The good angels' choice is freer, since choice that cannot serve sin is freer; their impeccability comes from grace, not nature, as only God is impeccable by nature (c3); grace confirmed, not weakened, free choice, so Jerome's 'all can turn either way' refers to the state of creation (c4). Demons keep keen knowledge from nature, experience, and revelation (c5). Magic works through demons, whose power God gives to deceive the deceitful, warn the faithful, or test the just, as Pharaoh's magicians failed at the gnats (c6); matter obeys God, not demons (c7). Angels are not creators but use hidden seeds placed by God in the elements (c8–9). What demons could do by nature they may be prevented from doing by God's prohibition, and humans cannot discern these limits (c10).
claims: Good angels are confirmed in good; bad angels are obstinate in evil.
Both retain free choice, which in the bad is corrupted.
Freedom that cannot serve sin is greater freedom.
Angelic impeccability comes from grace, not nature.
Demons have keen knowledge and power only by God's permission.
Angels are not creators; God alone creates through hidden seeds.

pl-l2d8.summary: Asks whether angels have bodies. Some, citing Augustine, hold angels have aerial bodies, the good keeping fine ones and the bad having them thickened at the fall; others say Augustine was reporting others' view, and many Catholic writers teach angels are incorporeal, assuming bodies for their ministry and laying them aside (c1). God appeared to humans in bodily forms (c2), but Augustine left unresolved how angels produced such appearances; what is certain is that God's immutable essence was never seen, all theophanies being made through creatures by angels (c3). Demons do not enter human souls substantially, since only God can enter the mind, but act by suggestion and oppression; they are 'cast out' when prevented from harming (Gennadius, Bede) (c4).
claims: Opinions differ on whether angels have bodies; many teach they are incorporeal and assume bodies.
God appeared in bodily forms through creatures and angels.
God's essence was never seen by mortals, being immutable and so invisible.
Demons do not substantially enter the soul; only God can.
Demons act on humans by suggestion and oppression.

pl-l2d9.summary: Treats the angelic orders. There are nine in three triads, reflecting the Trinity (Dionysius) (c1). An order is a multitude of spirits alike in a gift of grace; each order is named from its function (c2). Names are given for our sake from gifts held more excellently, though all share all gifts; charity ranks above knowledge, and whoever loves more knows more (c3). The orders did not exist before the fall, since they are defined by gifts given to those who stood; the fallen are said to come from every order because they would have belonged to each (c4). Angels within an order are not equal (c5). There is no tenth human order; humans are assumed into the angelic orders by merit, restoring what fell (c6). Gregory holds the saved number as many as the angels who remained; Augustine says no fewer than those who fell (c7).
claims: There are nine angelic orders in three triads.
An order is defined by a shared gift of grace.
The orders were formed after the fall, by gifts given to those who stood.
Angels within one order differ in dignity.
Humans are assumed into the angelic orders by merit.
The number of the saved is known to God.

pl-l2d10.summary: Asks whether all angels are sent on missions. Some hold the higher orders always stand within (Dan 7:10; Dionysius); others, citing Isa 6:6 and Heb 1:14, hold all are sent, some often by office, others rarely for special causes, and that angels are spirits by nature and messengers by office (c1). Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael are names of spirits, perhaps applied according to the task, as demons' names may be. Higher angels, even when sent, never leave God's presence and contemplation; or the highest orders stay, the middle relay commands, and the lowest are sent, taking the name of their office, as the 'Seraph' sent to Isaiah (c2).
claims: Opinions differ on whether all angels are sent.
'Angel' names an office, not a nature.
Angels sent never leave God's presence and contemplation.
Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael are names of spirits, not orders.
Angels may take the name of the office they perform.

pl-l2d11.summary: Treats the angels' relation to humans. Each of the elect has a guardian angel from birth (Matt 18:10; Jerome), and, per Gregory, each person has a good angel to guard and a bad one to test; one angel may serve several people (c1). Do good angels advance in merit and reward until judgment? Some hold they grow in knowledge and love, their charity being both merit and reward, and the angels grew in knowledge of the Incarnation (with Haymo, the higher knew it partially beforehand, the lower when fulfilled). Others hold they grew only in external knowledge, not in contemplation or charity. Lombard finds the first view more probable; statements that angels 'know all' refer to beatifying knowledge of the Trinity (c2).
claims: Each of the elect has a guardian angel; each person also has a testing demon.
One angel may guard several people.
The angels came to know the mystery of the Incarnation more fully after its fulfillment.
Lombard holds it more probable that angels advance in knowledge and other goods until judgment.

pl-l2d12.summary: Turns from angels to the work of the six days. With the angels God created unformed matter, chaos, before any day (c1). The Fathers differ: Augustine seems to hold that all was created at once, while Gregory, Jerome, Bede, and others hold that matter was formed over six days, which fits Genesis better (c2). Unformed matter is called earth, abyss, and water; the darkness was absence of light (c3), though 'darkness' can also mean darkened air, a creature (c4). Matter was not wholly formless but in a form of confusion before the form of disposition, located where the world now is; God formed six kinds of things in six days and rested on the seventh by ceasing to make new kinds, though he still works (c5). Alcuin gives four modes of divine working: disposing in the Word, creating matter from nothing, distinguishing in six days, and renewing natures from seeds (c6).
claims: Unformed matter was created before the six days.
The Fathers disagree whether formation was simultaneous or over six days; the latter fits Genesis better.
Darkness as privation is nothing; as darkened air it is a creature.
Unformed matter had a form of confusion before the form of disposition.
God's rest means ceasing to make new kinds, not ceasing to work.
God works by disposing, creating, distinguishing, and renewing.

pl-l2d13.summary: Treats the first day. Creation's distinction began with light (c1), which can be read spiritually as the formation of angelic nature by conversion to God, or, more probably, as a corporeal luminous body made from preexisting matter (c2), made where the sun now shines and circling to make day and night (c3). 'Day' has several senses; the first day began in full light and had evening but no morning (c4). Days are naturally counted morning to morning, but mystically evening to evening, signifying the fall into darkness and return to light through Christ; the first light may have become the sun (c5). 'God said' means not temporal or vocal speech but the eternal Word, in which God disposed from eternity what is made in time (c6). The Father works 'through' the Son and Spirit not as instruments but together with them, the phrasing showing the Father's authority (c7).
claims: Creation's distinction began with light.
The first light may be read as angelic nature or, more probably, as a corporeal light.
The first day had evening but no morning.
Counting days from evening signifies redemption from darkness to light.
God's speech in creation is the eternal Word, not temporal sound.
The Father works with, not through instruments of, the Son and Spirit.

pl-l2d14.summary: Treats the second through fourth days. The firmament is the starry heaven between the waters (c1–2), perhaps made of water like crystal (c3); God can suspend waters above it, whether ice-like or vaporous, and Augustine leaves open whether 'firmament' means the upper heaven or the air (c4). Scripture teaches what profits salvation, not heaven's shape, and 'firmament' need not mean immobile (c5). 'It was good' is omitted on the second day perhaps because two signifies division (c6). On the third day the waters below heaven were gathered into one bed, the air cleared, and the dry land appeared and brought forth plants (c7). The waters were gathered as the earth sank or they condensed; all connect to the great sea (c8). The first three days distinguished the four elements; the next three adorned them, heaven first with the stars, which serve human needs; man was made from earth but for heaven (c9). 'Times' made by the stars are seasons and hours, since time existed before them (c10).
claims: The firmament is the starry heaven between the waters.
God can suspend waters above the heavens.
Scripture teaches what profits salvation.
The first three days distinguished the elements; the next three adorned them.
Man was made from earth but for heaven.
Time existed before the stars; the stars mark seasons and hours.
On the third day the waters were gathered and the dry land produced plants.

pl-l2d15.summary: Treats the fifth and sixth days and the seventh. Fish and birds were made from water (c1), land animals on the sixth day (c2). Harmful animals were created harmless and became harmful through sin, to punish vice or test virtue (c3); creatures arising from decay were created potentially (c4). Man was made last as lord; Lombard has followed the six-day view because it fits Genesis and the Church favors it (c5). The alternative, Augustine's simultaneous creation, holds that Moses described successively what God did at once, the six days being six kinds made partly formally, partly causally (c6). God rested on the seventh day not from weariness but by ceasing to make new kinds of creatures, while continuing to sustain and govern them (John 5:17) (c7). Creation was completed on the sixth day; all is good and very good as a whole (c8–9). The seventh day was 'completed' by being blessed and sanctified, a mystical blessing grounding the week (c10).
claims: Fish and birds were made from water; land animals on the sixth day.
Harmful creatures became harmful through sin.
Lombard follows the six-day view as fitting Genesis and favored by the Church.
Augustine held simultaneous creation, described successively for a simple people.
All creation is good, and very good as a whole.
The seventh day was blessed and sanctified.
God's rest means ceasing to create new kinds, while continuing to sustain and govern creation.

pl-l2d16.summary: Begins the treatment of man: why he was created, how established, what he was, how he fell, and how restored (c1). 'Let us make man in our image' shows one operation and one substance of the three persons, spoken to the Son and Spirit, not angels (c2). The image may be the uncreated Trinity, improperly so called, or created in man; man himself is the image, not only made to the image, and the image and likeness are in the mind, image in memory, understanding, and love, likeness in innocence and justice or in the soul's immortality; man is image of the whole Trinity (c3). Man is image and made 'to the image,' unequal; the Son is image as equal; man's upright stature is a bodily sign of the rational soul (c4).
claims: 'Let us make' shows one operation of the Trinity.
Man is the image of the whole Trinity, by his soul.
The image lies in memory, understanding, and love; the likeness in innocence and justice.
The Son is image by equality; man is image by unequal likeness.
Upright stature signals the rational soul.

pl-l2d17.summary: Partial summary based on 6 of 7 chapters; c7 (on the tree of knowledge) has no paragraphs of its own, its text currently lying within c6. Treats the soul's origin and paradise. The soul's making is described in Gen 2:7 (c1); Augustine thought the first soul was created outside the body, others within it, but all other souls are created by being infused (c2). Adam was made at once as an adult by higher causes, God's will, not against nature (c3). Man was made outside paradise and placed in it, showing it was a gift of grace (c4). Lombard prefers that paradise is both a real place and a figure of the Church (c5). The tree of life kept the body in stable health; the tree of knowledge was not evil but named from the experience of disobedience; God forbade a good thing so that obedience itself would be the good (c6).
claims: Souls are created by God and infused into bodies.
Adam was made as an adult by God's will, not by seminal causes.
Paradise was a gift of grace and a real place as well as a figure.
The tree of life preserved bodily health.
The forbidden tree was good; disobedience was the evil.
