pl-l2d18.summary: Treats the formation of woman and the origin of souls. Woman was formed from Adam's rib so that humanity have one principle, confounding the devil's pride and imaging God as principle (c1); from his side, as companion, neither ruler nor servant (c2); while he slept, without pain, figuring the Church formed from the sacraments flowing from Christ's side (c3); from the rib alone, multiplied by divine power, angels ministering but not creating (c4). The causes of all things are in God's eternal disposition; seminal reasons in creatures are secondary and mutable (c5). Some causes are hidden in God alone; woman's formation from the rib was such a work beyond nature, signifying grace, possible but not necessary in nature (c6). Souls are neither propagated from parents nor created all at once, but created by God and infused into bodies formed in the womb (Gennadius, Jerome) (c7).
claims: Humanity has a single principle, Adam.
Woman was made as man's companion.
Eve from Adam's side figures the Church from Christ's side.
Only God creates; angels only minister.
Primordial causes are in God; seminal reasons in creatures.
Miracles have causes hidden in God and do not contradict nature.
Each soul is created by God and infused; traducianism and preexistence are rejected.

pl-l2d19.summary: Treats man's bodily state before sin. There are three states: before sin able to die and not to die; after sin unable not to die; finally unable to die, by grace (c1). The first body was animal, needing food; sin made it 'dead,' bound to die; the risen body will be spiritual and unable to die (c2–3). Man's mortality was natural, his ability not to die a gift of grace through the tree of life (c4). Opinions differ whether he could have lived without that tree (c5). Adam's immortality was conditional on food and obedience and would have been perfected by the tree of life; Lombard leaves open how this fits Augustine's other statements (c6).
claims: Man has three states: able not to die, unable not to die, unable to die.
The first body was animal and needed food.
Sin made the body subject to necessary death.
Original immortality was a gift of grace through the tree of life.
Adam's immortality depended on obedience.

pl-l2d20.summary: Treats procreation and the state of children before sin. Without sin, the first parents would have procreated in paradise without concupiscence or pain, the members obeying the will; marriage was an office for the healthy and became a remedy for the sick (c1). They did not unite in paradise because they fell soon or God had not yet commanded it (c2). When humans would have passed to the higher life, together or in succession, is uncertain (c3). Children would have been born small and probably grown over time, which is natural, not a fault; needing food before sin was natural, and only immoderate hunger is a punishment (c4). They would also have grown in knowledge, since not every lack of knowledge is penal ignorance (c5). God prepared two goods for man, temporal and eternal, giving the first and promising the second to be merited by keeping a command added to natural reason (c6).
claims: Procreation in paradise would have been without concupiscence.
Marriage is an office before sin and a remedy after it.
Children would have grown gradually in body and knowledge, without fault.
Not every lack of knowledge is ignorance as punishment.
God gave man a temporal good and promised an eternal one, to be merited by obedience.

pl-l2d21.summary: Treats the temptation of the first parents. The devil, envying man's capacity to rise by humble obedience where he had fallen by pride, attacked the woman as the weaker part of human nature (c1). Unable to use violence, he used fraud, permitted to appear only in a form fitting his malice, the serpent (c2), which is called most cunning because his spirit filled it; he did not choose it but used the animal permitted him, speaking through it as an unknowing instrument, the will to harm being his and the power God's (c3–4). He began with a question, exploited the woman's doubt ('lest perhaps we die'), denied God's threat, and promised likeness to God and knowledge, tempting by gluttony, vainglory, and avarice (c5). Temptation is exterior or interior; interior temptation from the flesh is not without sin (c6). Man, falling by another's suggestion, could be helped to pardon, while the devil, who fell by himself, could not; human nature wholly fell and so was in part redeemed to replace the fallen angels (c7). The command reached the woman through the man, and the first parents could speak without learning (c8).
claims: The devil tempted out of envy, attacking the weaker part of human nature.
He was permitted to tempt only through the serpent, a form fitting his malice.
The temptation proceeded from question through doubt to denial, by gluttony, vainglory, and avarice.
Interior temptation from the flesh is not without sin; temptation from the enemy is sin only with consent.
Man's sin is remediable because he fell by another; the devil's is not.
Redeemed humans fill the place of fallen angels.

pl-l2d22.summary: Treats the root and degree of the first sin. Pride preceded not the temptation but the act: once the devil spoke, pride and love of her own power entered the woman's mind, so she sinned by suggestion (c1). She believed and willed equality with God (c2). Adam was not seduced, since he did not believe the devil, though he may have thought the sin venial and wished to try the tree (c3). The woman sinned more, believing and willing likeness to God and sinning against herself, neighbor, and God, though both were equal in excusing themselves; Adam consented so as not to grieve his wife (c4). Ignorance excuses only when invincible; known commands leave no excuse; the evil consent arose from good free choice, through the devil's persuasion and man's consent (c5). The will preceded the act, but no evil will preceded that will, which was itself iniquity (c6).
claims: Pride entered the woman after the devil's suggestion, not before.
The woman believed the devil; Adam was not seduced.
The woman sinned more than Adam.
Ignorance of a known command does not excuse.
The first evil will arose from free choice and the devil's persuasion and was itself iniquity.

pl-l2d23.summary: Treats why God permitted the temptation and man's original knowledge. God permitted it because resisting temptation is more glorious than being untemptable, and man could resist with God's help; God created those he foresaw would be evil because he foresaw the good he would make of their evils, their evil will being their own; why he did not make them unable to sin he knows (c1). Man was given at creation, not by study, knowledge suited to his first perfection (c2): of creatures, which he did not lose; of the Creator, by inward contemplation of his presence, between our faith and the saints' future vision; and of himself and his duties (c3). He was told what to do but not shown his future, so he did not foreknow his fall (c4).
claims: Resisting temptation is more glorious than being unable to be tempted.
God created those he foresaw would be evil because he would bring good from their evil.
Man received knowledge at creation, not by study.
Before the fall man knew creatures, the Creator by inward contemplation, and himself.
Man did not foreknow his fall.

pl-l2d24.summary: Treats man's original grace, free choice, and how sin arises in the soul. Man received at creation a help by which he could stand but not advance to merit without further grace; he had the ability if he willed, not the will to use it (c1). That help was uncorrupted free choice, upright will, and intact natural powers (c2). Free choice is the faculty of reason and will by which good is chosen with grace assisting, evil without it (c3). The soul has sensuality, shared with beasts, and reason, whose higher part contemplates eternal reasons (wisdom) and lower part governs temporal things (knowledge), one mind with two offices (c4–5). Temptation in each person mirrors the fall: sensuality is the serpent, lower reason the woman, higher reason the man, joined in a spiritual marriage (c6–8). Sin held only in sensual motion is very light; when lower reason consents in delight of thought, the woman eats; when higher reason consents to the deed, the man eats too and the sin is mortal; lingering delight in thought is also mortal (c9–12). 'Sensuality' can also name the lower reason (c13).
claims: Before sin man could stand without further grace but not advance to merit.
Free choice is the faculty of reason and will choosing good with grace, evil without it.
Reason has a higher part for eternal things and a lower part for temporal things.
Sensuality, lower reason, and higher reason correspond to serpent, woman, and man.
Sin in sensual motion alone is very light; consent of higher reason to the deed is mortal.
Lingering delight in a sinful thought, even without will to act, can be mortal.

pl-l2d25.summary: Treats free choice in its states. Free choice is free judgment concerning the will and bears on future contingents in our power (c1); in God it is his free, wise, omnipotent will, not as in creatures (c2). The blessed have free choice though unable to sin, and that inability makes it freer (c3–4). There are three liberties: the first able to sin and not to sin, the middle able to sin and unable not to sin, the last able not to sin and unable to sin (c5); and four states: before sin, after sin without grace, under grace, and in glory (c6). Sin wounded natural goods and removed gratuitous ones, like the man stripped by robbers, so man lost freedom from sin and misery, not free choice itself (c7). Freedom from necessity is natural and never lost; freedom from sin is restored by grace; freedom from misery belongs to paradise and glory. Lombard holds the freedom for evil and freedom for good are one free choice named by different causes; fallen choice is freer for evil than for good (c8). Freedom from necessity is by nature, from sin and misery by grace, which precedes and prepares the will (c9).
claims: Free choice concerns future contingents within our power.
Free choice in God differs from free choice in creatures.
Inability to sin makes free choice freer, not abolished.
Free choice passes through four states: innocence, fall, grace, and glory.
Sin lost freedom from sin and misery, not freedom from necessity.
The freedom for evil and the freedom for good are one free choice, named by different causes.
Grace precedes and prepares the will to will good.

pl-l2d26.summary: Partial summary based on 7 of 11 chapters; c8 to c11, as the EDF divides the text, are encoded in this repository as Distinction 27, chapters 1 to 4, and are summarized there. Treats operating and cooperating grace. Operating grace prepares the will to will good; cooperating grace helps it not to will in vain; grace makes the will good, not makes it a will (c1). Will is an uncompelled motion of the mind; Rom 9:16 gives all to God, who prevents the unwilling and follows the willing, so good will follows grace (c2). The grace preventing the will is faith with charity, itself freely given, the cause of justification (c3). Good will precedes some gifts and is preceded by others; faith precedes good will in cause and nature, not time; some good thought precedes faith, but not the good will of right living, which requires faith working through love (c4–5). Understanding precedes desire, and desire precedes delight in the good, which comes through faith and charity (c6). So Augustine's statements agree: goods may precede justifying grace, but none merit it; free choice can do natural goods like farming without cooperating grace (c7).
claims: Operating grace prepares the will; cooperating grace helps it accomplish good.
Good will follows grace and does not lead it.
The grace preventing the will is faith with charity.
Faith precedes good will in cause and nature, not in time.
No merits precede justifying grace.
Free choice can do natural goods without cooperating grace.

pl-l2d27.summary: Treats the nature of grace, virtue, and merit. Operating and cooperating grace may be one gift named by its effects (c1). Answering how grace merits and whether it is a virtue or an act requires Augustine's three kinds of goods: great (virtues), middle (powers of the soul, including free choice), and least (bodily forms) (c2–4). Virtue is a good quality of mind by which one lives rightly, which no one misuses, and which God alone works in man; faith is God's gift, not from free choice (c5). Since every motion of the mind is from free choice, some hold virtue is a quality informing the soul, not a motion, watering free choice like rain so that good motion and good work arise (c6). Grace is the principal cause of merit, without excluding free choice (c7). The first merit is a good motion from grace and free choice, like believing and loving, which are both merits and God's gifts (c8). Faith merits by its act when charity, the Holy Spirit, is present (c9). God crowns his own gifts; 'virtue' in Augustine's 'good use of free choice' means its act (c10). Grace is from God alone, good use from God and man (c11). Others hold virtues are good interior motions of the mind; Lombard leaves the question to the reader (c12).
claims: Operating and cooperating grace may be one gift with two effects.
Free choice is a middle good; its good use is a great good.
Virtue is a good quality of mind that God alone works in man.
On one view, virtue is a quality informing the soul, and the good motion arises from virtue and free choice.
Grace is the principal cause of merit, without excluding free choice.
When God crowns our merits he crowns his own gifts.
Lombard leaves undecided whether virtues are qualities or motions of the mind.

pl-l2d28.summary: Rejects Pelagianism. Free choice without prevenient and helping grace does not suffice for justice and salvation, and grace is not given for merits (c1). Augustine's account of the Pelagians: they claim man can fulfill all commands without grace, which only makes this easier; they reduce grace to nature, law, and teaching; they deny charity is God's gift, undermine the Church's prayers, and deny original sin in infants (c2). Pelagian arguments drawn from Augustine's early works are answered from his Retractationes: his texts did not exclude grace or were aimed at the Manichees; the power to change the will is God-given; willing and doing are both God's and ours; faith is the Spirit's gift; and the natural aptitude for faith and charity is actualized only by grace (c3). Jerome's confession: we always need God's help, and man can always sin and not sin, against both Mani and Jovinian (c4).
claims: Free choice without grace does not suffice for salvation.
Grace is not given according to merits.
Pelagians reduced grace to nature, law, and teaching, and denied original sin.
Augustine's early statements, rightly read, do not support Pelagianism.
The mind's natural aptitude for faith and charity is actualized only by grace.
We always need God's help, and man can always sin and not sin.

pl-l2d29.summary: Treats grace and virtue before the fall and the expulsion from paradise. Before sin man needed operating and cooperating grace, not to free his will but to prepare it to will good effectively; he could stand without it but not advance (c1). Against those who deny it, Adam had the virtues before sin and lost them by sinning (c2). He was expelled from paradise as punishment, God's words about the tree of life expressing his unworthiness (c3–4). The cherubim and flaming sword are literally an angelic guard and spiritually charity and temporal suffering, through which alone one returns to life (c5). The first parents ate of the tree of life before sin, which perhaps conferred immortality only if eaten often (c6).
claims: Before sin man needed grace to prepare, not to free, his will.
Adam had virtues before sin and lost them by it.
The expulsion from paradise was a punishment fitting man's unworthiness.
Return to life is through charity and enduring temporal suffering.
The first parents ate of the tree of life before sin.

pl-l2d30.summary: Begins the treatment of original sin. Sin and death passed from the first man to all (c1–2). Some read Rom 5:12 of Adam's actual disobedience spreading by imitation, the Pelagian error; but Adam is the origin, not just the example, of sin, which passes by propagation (c3–4) to all begotten through concupiscence (c5). Against the view that original sin is mere liability to punishment, neither fault nor punishment (c6), authorities show it is fault (c7). It is the tinder of sin (fomes), concupiscence, the law of the members and languor of nature (c8), meaning not the act of desiring but a defect, hidden in infants and lessened but never ended in this life (c9). All sinned in Adam as in matter and were made sinners, freed only by baptism (c10); original sin came from Adam's actual disobedience and so from his will (c11–13). Answering the objection that Adam could not contain all human substance, Lombard holds all were in him materially and causally, by seminal reason, human substance multiplying in itself without food becoming the truth of human nature, which alone will rise (c13–15).
claims: Original sin passes by propagation, not only imitation.
Original sin is fault, not mere liability to punishment.
Original sin is the tinder of sin, concupiscence, understood as a defect.
All sinned in Adam as in matter.
Original sin proceeded from Adam's actual sin and so from will.
All human bodily substance was in Adam causally and grows by self-multiplication; only the truth of human nature rises.

pl-l2d31.summary: Treats how original sin is transmitted. Is it through the soul, the flesh, or both (c1)? Some held that souls are propagated like bodies, so a sinful soul begets a sinful soul (c2). The Catholic faith rejects this: only flesh is propagated, so original sin passes through the flesh alone. It is concupiscence as a defect, which is in the soul but arises there through the flesh's corruption (c3). Since the fall, union cannot occur without lust, which is a defect and is fault unless excused by the goods of marriage. Flesh conceived in lust is polluted, and the soul contracts the stain when infused (c4). The flesh holds the cause of sin, not fault; sin, a privation, dwells in the flesh as cause, and the soul is not propagated (c5). That cause is a pollution of the flesh contracted in conception, shown by its effect on the soul, as a faulty jar sours wine. Baptized parents still transmit original sin because they beget by their carnal, not their spiritual, birth (c6). Original sin is named from the law of our origin, conception in lust. Christ's flesh descended from Adam but was conceived without lust and so without sin. Since the soul is infused only into the formed body, the flesh first contracts the cause and the soul then the sin (c7).
claims: Original sin is transmitted through the flesh alone, since souls are not propagated.
Original sin is concupiscence, arising in the soul through the corrupted flesh.
Since the fall, union cannot occur without lust; flesh conceived in lust is polluted.
The flesh holds the cause of sin, not fault; the soul contracts the stain when infused.
Baptized parents transmit original sin by their carnal birth.
Christ was conceived without lust and so without sin.

pl-l2d32.summary: Treats the remission of original sin and related questions. Concupiscence remains after baptism, but its guilt is loosed and it is weakened so that it does not reign; it passes in guilt and remains in act (c1). It is probable, though disputed, that the flesh is also cleansed in baptism (c2). Concupiscence as punishment has God as author, as fault the devil or man (c3). The soul is justly held to original sin because the body's corruption is the punishment of sin, not its cause (c4). Original sin is necessary because unavoidable and voluntary because it came from Adam's will (c5). God joins souls to bodies that will stain them by the depth of his judgments, keeping the original law of human condition (c6). The soul is not wholly as God made it, for its natural goodness is vitiated but not lost, and evil exists only in good (c7). Souls probably differ by creation in natural gifts, but wit does not decide reward or punishment (c8).
claims: Baptism looses the guilt of concupiscence and weakens it, but does not remove it.
Concupiscence after baptism is punishment, not fault.
God authors punishment, not fault.
Original sin is both necessary and voluntary.
The soul keeps its natural goodness, vitiated by sin.
Natural ability does not determine reward or punishment.

pl-l2d33.summary: Concludes the treatment of original sin. Do the sins of other ancestors also pass to infants (c1)? Augustine discussed it only as opinion: Adam's one sin contained many sins, but infants, whose punishment is the mildest, are bound only by original sin. They suffer no fire or worm of conscience, only lack of the vision of God, and Scripture's plurals stand for the one sin (c2). Adam's sin was not the gravest, since the sin against the Holy Spirit is graver; it corrupted all nature because all nature was then in one man (c3). Adam and Eve were forgiven through penance, though they remained subject to death (c4). The fathers' sins visited on their descendants (Exod 20:5) agree with Ezekiel 18: children are punished for imitating their fathers. Mystically, the four generations are the stages of sin, and the first motions of thought are not punished eternally (c5).
claims: Infants are bound only by Adam's sin, not their ancestors' actual sins.
Unbaptized infants suffer only the lack of the vision of God.
Adam's sin was not graver than the sin against the Holy Spirit.
Adam and Eve were saved through penance.
Children are punished for imitating their fathers' sins, not for those sins as such.
First motions of thought are not punished eternally.

pl-l2d34.summary: Begins the treatment of actual sin. It lays out the questions of sin's origin, subject, definition, modes, and kinds (c1). The first origin of sin was a good thing, the good nature of angel and man, since no evil preceded the first evil will (c2). That will, failing from the immutable good, causes later evils, both sins and punishments (c3). Evil exists only in good, since it is the privation of good. An evil nature is a good that is evil: an evil man is good as a man and evil as unjust (c4). So the dialecticians' rule about contraries fails for good and evil. Isaiah's 'woe to those who call good evil' condemns praising vice, not this way of speaking. Iniquity is against the law, written or natural (c5).
claims: The first origin of sin was a good nature.
The first evil will, failing from the immutable good, causes later sins and punishments.
Evil is the privation of good and exists only in good.
An evil nature is a good that is evil.
Good and evil, unlike other contraries, coexist in one subject.

pl-l2d35.summary: Defines sin. Augustine defines it as every word, deed, or desire against God's law, and as the will to keep or obtain what justice forbids. Ambrose defines it as transgression and disobedience (c1). Views differ on whether sin is the will alone, the will and its acts, or neither. Lombard teaches that sin is an evil interior and exterior act, but consists chiefly in the will (c2). Some hold that evil acts are good insofar as they are acts and from God, and sins insofar as they are inordinate, and that as sin they are nothing. On this view, adultery names an act together with its vice, omissions signify acts of the will, and sin is privation actively, not passively (c3). Sin, though no substance, corrupts the soul, as fasting weakens the body: it strips away the virtues and wounds natural goods (c4). Sin removes us from God not by place but by unlikeness, and it also deprived the body of immortality (c5). Sin is privation as cause, punishment as effect; punishment is from God, fault from creatures (c6).
claims: Sin is every word, deed, or desire against God's law.
Sin consists chiefly in the will, from which evil works proceed.
On one view, evil acts are good as acts and sinful as inordinate.
Sin, though no substance, corrupts the soul.
Distance from God by sin is unlikeness, not place.
Sin is privation as cause; punishment is privation as effect.

pl-l2d36.summary: Treats sins that are also punishments of sins. Between the first apostasy and eternal fire, intermediate sins are both, and unrepented sin brings on further sin (c1). Such a sin is a punishment not as sin: the corruption of nature that follows God's desertion is the punishment, and it is from God, while the sin that causes it is not (c2). A sin is the punishment of a prior sin and the cause of a later one, so crimes are avenged by crimes (c3–4). Some things done by necessity, such as the inability to do the good one wills, are just punishment from man's condemnation (c5). Envy, anger, desire, and fear are sins that are also punishments. Augustine on sins done by necessity concerns this state of misery and includes venial sins, while Jerome concerns mortal sins, which grace enables one to avoid. On the first view, acts are good by being, by kind, and perfectly by cause and end (c6).
claims: Some sins are also punishments of earlier sins.
Such sins are punishments from God not as sins but as corruptions of nature.
Unrepented sin leads to further sin through God's desertion.
Venial sins are unavoidable in this life; mortal sins are avoidable with grace.
Acts can be good by being, by kind, and by cause and end.

pl-l2d37.summary: Presents the opposing view that evil will and acts are in no way good or from God. Sin is 'nothing' because it leads away from true being. 'All that is is good' applies only to natures and what is concreated with them, and acts are not natures, so the things by which men are evil are not from God (c1). The objection is that the first view is trivial, since nothing has no author. Augustine also says iniquity is not substance but a perversion made by man. Lombard leaves the choice between the two views to the reader. All agree that God is the author of punishments but not of sins, as 'God did not make death' means he did not make the sin for which death is inflicted (c2).
claims: On the second view, evil acts are not natures and are in no way from God.
'All that is is good' applies to natures and substances.
Iniquity is a perversion made by man, not a substance.
Lombard leaves the choice between the two views to the reader.
God is author of punishments, not of sins.

pl-l2d38.summary: Treats the will and its end. A will is judged right or wrong by its end. The end of good will is beatitude, which is God, and every precept is referred to charity (c1). Whoever makes charity his end makes God his end; Christ is the end of the law, and the Trinity is one end (c2). Good wills have their own subordinate ends, all referred to one end of ends. Augustine's warning against two ends forbids ends not referred to one another, and temporal goods may be sought for the sake of eternal life (c3). Will regards what we will, while intention regards that for which we will it, and 'intention' can mean either. Whether these are one will or two is disputed, but the will is always judged by its end (c4).
claims: The will is judged right or wrong by its end.
The end of good will is beatitude, which is God; charity is the end of every precept.
The Trinity is one final end.
Subordinate ends are permitted when referred to the final end.
Will regards what we will; intention regards that for which we will it.

pl-l2d39.summary: Asks why the will, a natural power, is not always good, since natural powers stay good however vitiated. The will as power is never sin; the will as act is sin when inordinate (c1). Willing aims at obtaining or rejecting, so to will evil is evil, while knowing evil is not. On the other view, only the power of willing is natural (c2). How does sinful man naturally will good? Some posit two motions: the natural will for good, the spark of reason never extinguished even in Cain, and the will that serves sin. Grace crushes the second and frees the first. Others posit one will, good in willing good and evil in willing evil (c3).
claims: Will as natural power is never sin; will as act can be.
To will evil is evil; to know evil is not.
The spark of reason always wills good, even in Cain.
Grace frees the natural will for good from the will that serves sin.
Some posit one will with two directions.

pl-l2d40.summary: Asks whether acts, like the will, are judged good or evil by their end. Acts are simply good when they have a good cause and intention, since intention makes the good work and faith directs it. Some hold all acts indifferent, and others divide them three ways. With Augustine (Contra mendacium), Lombard holds that acts are judged by intention and cause, except those that are sins in themselves, such as theft, adultery, and false witness, which may not be done for any seemingly good end. So every good act is good by its end, but not every evil act is evil by its end. Some add that such acts never have a truly good cause (c1).
claims: Acts are simply good when they have a good cause and intention.
Intention makes the good work, and faith directs intention.
Acts are judged by intention and cause, except those that are sins in themselves.
Acts evil in themselves may not be done for any seemingly good end.
Every good act is good by its end; not every evil act is evil by its end.

pl-l2d41.summary: Partial summary based on 4 of 6 chapters; the EDF divides the same text into six chapters, so no text is missing (c3 here covers the EDF's c3 to c5, and c4 its c6). Asks whether all works of those without faith are sins. Some hold that they are ('whatever is not from faith is sin'), and that such works are good in kind but evil by affection. Others hold that works supporting nature are always good, and that a 'good work' can mean one rewardable for life (c1). 'Good' has many senses, so an act of natural piety without faith can be good, though not rewardable (c2). Augustine's sayings that sin is only voluntary and only in the will concern chiefly the first sin. Yet even sins of ignorance and weakness involve the will, so sin cannot exist without will (c3). Evil will is itself voluntary sin, and will is the first cause of sinning (c4).
claims: Some hold all works without faith are sins; others that natural works can be good though not meritorious.
'Good' is said in many ways; only intention directed by faith merits life.
Sin cannot exist without will, even in ignorance or weakness.
Will is the first cause of sin.

_metadata.note: pl-l2d41c5 and pl-l2d41c6 have no files of their own: the TEI divides this distinction into four chapters, with pl-l2d41c3 covering the EDF's c3 to c5 (its question-title combines their three titles) and pl-l2d41c4 corresponding to the EDF's c6. No text is missing

pl-l2d42.summary: Evil will and evil act concerning the same thing may be held one sin, enlarged by the act; two commands can be broken by one transgression (c1). Sin can remain in guilt after it passes in act (c2). Reatus means fault, punishment, or obligation to punishment; mortal sin merits eternal death, and venial sin is easily forgiven (c3). Sins are variously distinguished: all mortal sins come from cupidity or fear (Augustine on Ps 79); sin is committed in thought, word, or deed (Jerome), sometimes with habit as a fourth mode, figured by Lazarus four days dead; and sin is against God, neighbor, or oneself (c4). Delictum and peccatum may differ as deserting good and doing evil, or as sin in ignorance and knowing sin, though the terms are used interchangeably (c5). There are seven capital vices, from which all evils spring (c6). Pride is the root of all sin, with four species (c7). Pride and cupidity are each roots of every kind of sin, each sometimes giving rise to the other (c8).
claims: Will and act concerning one thing may be one sin.
Sin can remain in guilt after it passes in act.
Mortal sin merits eternal death; venial sin is easily forgiven.
All mortal sins arise from cupidity or fear; sin is in thought, word, or deed, and against God, neighbor, or self.
There are seven capital vices.
Pride and cupidity are each roots of every kind of sin.

pl-l2d43.summary: Treats the sin against the Holy Spirit, which is not forgiven here or hereafter. Some identify it with despair and obstinacy, which offend the Spirit's goodness. They differ on whether every such sin is meant and forgiven rarely, or only the impenitent kind, which is never forgiven. Augustine also defined it as an envious attack on grace and on the brotherhood after one has known God, adding later 'if one dies in it.' So no one in this life is to be despaired of, and all are to be prayed for. Ambrose identifies it with attributing the Spirit's works to Beelzebub. The sins against Father, Son, and Spirit are sins of weakness, ignorance, and malice, by appropriation (c1).
claims: The sin against the Holy Spirit is not forgiven here or hereafter.
It is identified with despair, obstinacy, impenitence, and envious attack on grace.
Whether one has committed it is known only after death, so all living sinners are to be prayed for.
Sins against Father, Son, and Spirit are sins of weakness, ignorance, and malice.

pl-l2d44.summary: Lombard asks about the source of the power to sin and the duty of resistance to power. He argues against those who assign the power of evil to humans or the devil that all power, even power to do harm, comes from God, with culpability lying in the will and in proud misuse (c1); he then reconciles this with Romans 13 by holding that resistance to any power commanding against God is obedience to God's ordination (c2).
claims: The power of sinning or harming is from God, though the will to do so is not.
Culpability lies in the abuse of power, not in power itself.
Romans 13 concerns lawful secular power; commands against God must be resisted.
Resisting a contra-divine command is obedience to the divine ordering.

pl-liber1.summary: Book 1 of the Sentences, on the Trinity and the one God. The prologue presents the work as a humble compilation of the Fathers' sentences in four books, to defend the faith, open theological questions, and teach the sacraments. Distinction 1 sets the plan of the whole work (things and signs) and the frui/uti framework, naming the Trinity as the sole object of enjoyment. Distinctions 2 to 3 establish one essence in three persons from Scripture, created vestiges, and the image of the Trinity in the mind. Distinctions 4 to 9 treat the Son's eternal generation by nature (the essence neither begets nor is begotten) and the truth, immutability, and simplicity of God. Distinctions 10 to 18 treat the Holy Spirit as mutual love and Gift, his procession from both, the visible and invisible missions, and Lombard's thesis that the Spirit is the charity by which we love God. Distinctions 19 to 21 establish coequality and mutual indwelling. Distinctions 22 to 34 analyze divine names and predication: personal, essential, temporal, and metaphorical names; 'person' as essence, hypostasis, or property; number words as exclusionary; the personal properties and notions as eternal relations identical with the persons and essence; 'principle'; temporal relations whose reality lies in creatures; and appropriations. Distinctions 35 to 48 treat the attributes: God's one knowledge named as foreknowledge, disposition, predestination, and providence; things present in his knowledge but not his essence; God's presence in all things; foreknowledge without imposed necessity; predestination and reprobation without merits, and hardening as the withholding of grace; omnipotence, which can do more and better than it does; and God's will, always fulfilled as good pleasure though its signs are resisted, permitting but not authoring evil, and fulfilled even through evil wills, as in Christ's passion. Throughout, Lombard gathers and harmonizes Augustine, Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, and John Damascene, distinguishing senses, reconciling apparent conflicts, confessing ineffability, and at times leaving hard questions open.
claims: Theology treats things and signs; the Trinity alone is to be enjoyed.
God is one simple, immutable essence in three coeternal, coequal persons distinguished by relations of origin.
The Son is eternally begotten by nature; the Spirit proceeds from both as their love and Gift.
The Holy Spirit is the charity by which we love God and neighbor.
Trinitarian terms are used by necessity of speech and must be interpreted by the reasons for speaking.
God's knowledge is one, immutable, and not caused by things; foreknowledge imposes no necessity.
Predestination and reprobation are not based on merits; hardening is the withholding of grace.
God can do more and better than he does; his power and will are one.
God's will (good pleasure) is always fulfilled; he permits but does not author evil, and brings good from it.

pl-liber2.summary: Summary of Book 2 (on creation, angels, man, grace, and sin), based on all 44 distinctions. It remains partial at the chapter level: Distinction 17 has one chapter not yet interpreted, and Distinctions 26 and 41 are divided differently in the TEI than in the EDF (the text of the EDF's d26c8 to c11 is encoded as d27c1 to c4, and d41 has four TEI chapters for the EDF's six), so no text is missing. Distinction 1 sets out creation from nothing by God's goodness alone, without change, against Plato, Aristotle, and an eternal world; rational creatures exist to know, love, and enjoy God, and the world for man. Distinctions 2 to 11 treat the angels: created with time and matter in the empyrean, good but not yet blessed, with free choice; divided by conversion through cooperating grace and aversion through pride; the good confirmed and blessed, the bad, under Lucifer, obstinate in the dark air; demons' knowledge and power limited by God; angelic bodies and theophanies; nine orders defined by gifts of grace; missions and guardian angels; and angelic progress in knowledge until judgment. Distinctions 12 to 15 treat the six days: unformed matter, the light of the first day, the firmament, the gathering of waters, the luminaries, animals, and God's rest; Lombard follows the six-day view as fitting Genesis while presenting Augustine's simultaneous creation. Distinctions 16 to 20 treat man: made in the image of the whole Trinity in mind, soul created by infusion, placed in paradise by grace with the trees of life and knowledge, woman formed from Adam's side as companion and figure of the Church, conditional immortality through the tree of life, and procreation without concupiscence, all ordered to an eternal good to be merited by obedience. Distinctions 21 to 23 treat the fall: the devil's envious temptation through the serpent, the woman's pride and belief, Adam's unseduced consent, their unequal guilt, God's reasons for permitting temptation, and man's original knowledge. Distinctions 24 to 29 treat free choice and grace: man's original grace to stand but not advance; free choice as the faculty of reason and will; sin's progress in the soul through sensuality, lower reason, and higher reason; the three liberties and four states of free choice; operating and cooperating grace, faith with charity as prevenient grace, virtue, and merit as God's gifts; the rejection of Pelagianism; and Adam's grace and virtues before the fall and his expulsion from paradise. Distinction 30 begins original sin: transmitted by propagation, not imitation, it is fault, namely the defect of concupiscence, contracted by all who were materially in Adam. Distinctions 31 to 33 complete original sin: it passes through the flesh alone, since souls are not propagated, by conception in lust; baptism looses its guilt and weakens concupiscence, which remains as punishment; infants are bound only by Adam's sin and suffer only the lack of the vision of God; Adam and Eve were saved by penance. Distinctions 34 to 37 treat actual sin: its first origin was a good nature, and evil, the privation of good, exists only in good; sin is every word, deed, or desire against God's law and consists chiefly in the will; Lombard reports without deciding whether evil acts are good insofar as they are acts or in no way from God; and some sins are punishments of earlier sins, God being the author of punishment but not of fault. Distinctions 38 to 40 treat will, intention, and end: the will is judged by its end, which is God loved in charity; the power of will is never sin, though its act may be; and acts are judged by intention, except those that are sins in themselves. Distinctions 41 to 43 treat the works of unbelievers, the voluntariness of sin, mortal and venial sin, the seven capital vices with pride and cupidity as roots, and the sin against the Holy Spirit. Distinction 44 holds that all power, even to sin, is from God while the guilt lies in the will, and that resisting a command against God is obedience to him.
claims: God alone creates from nothing, by goodness, not necessity.
All angels were created good; some fell by free, prideful aversion, others were confirmed by grace.
The world was formed over six days from unformed matter, though Augustine held simultaneous creation.
Man is the image of the Trinity in his mind; each soul is created by God and infused.
In paradise man had conditional immortality by grace and was to merit eternal life by obedience.
Man fell by the devil's suggestion, and so his sin is remediable.
Free choice without grace cannot will or do saving good; grace precedes and prepares the will, and merits are God's gifts.
Original sin is the fault of concupiscence, passed through the flesh to all conceived in lust and remitted in guilt by baptism.
Evil is the privation of good and exists only in good; sin consists chiefly in the will.
The will and its acts are judged by their end, except acts that are sins in themselves.
All power, even to sin, is from God; guilt lies in the will.

_metadata.note: All 44 distinctions are covered, but Distinctions 17, 26, and 41 are themselves partial (d17: one chapter not interpreted; d26 and d41: chapter divisions differ between the TEI and the EDF)

pl-l3d1.summary: Opens Book 3 with Gal 4:4: in the fullness of time, the time of grace, God sent his Son, and the Son's mission is the incarnation itself (prae). Only the Son became incarnate. It was fitting that God restore through Wisdom what he made through Wisdom, and that the one who is from another be sent. The Son took flesh so that the same person would be son in divinity and in humanity, one Son in two unconfused substances (c1). The Father or the Spirit could have become incarnate and still could (c2). The works of the Trinity are undivided: the whole Trinity worked the incarnation, but made it the flesh of the Word alone, as only the Son was born and crucified and only the Spirit descended as a dove (c3).
claims: The Son's mission is the incarnation.
Only the Son assumed flesh, fittingly, as Wisdom and as the one sent from another.
The Father or Spirit could have become incarnate.
The whole Trinity worked the incarnation, but only the Son assumed flesh.

pl-l3d2.summary: Teaches that because the whole of human nature was corrupted, the Word assumed the whole, soul and flesh with their properties, for what is not assumed is not healed. 'Humanity' names a substance, not a mere property, and in Christ human nature is not a common species but his own soul and body (c1). The Word assumed flesh through the mediation of the rational soul, since divine simplicity fits union with a body only through a rational nature. The union is inexplicable, and the assumed body was real and did not defile God, against those who held it was only apparent (c2). Soul and flesh were assumed at once, and the flesh was assumed in being conceived and conceived in being assumed (c3).
claims: The Word assumed the whole human nature, soul and flesh.
What is not assumed is not healed.
The Word assumed flesh through the mediation of the soul.
Christ's body was real.
Soul and flesh were assumed simultaneously, at conception.

pl-l3d3.summary: Treats the sanctification of Christ's flesh and of Mary. The Word's flesh was previously liable to sin but was cleansed by the Spirit before union, keeping only the penalty, taken by will. The Spirit cleansed Mary from sin and the tinder of sin and gave her power to conceive without a man (c1). Augustine excepts Mary from any question of sin (c2). Levi was tithed in Abraham but Christ was not, since Christ, though materially in Abraham's loins, did not descend through concupiscence by seminal reason (c3). Christ took the likeness of sinful flesh, like ours in penalty but not guilt. Augustine's 46 days do not mean the body was formed before union: the union was immediate, the members becoming visible later. The incarnate Word remained uncircumscribed (c4).
claims: Christ's flesh was cleansed before union and assumed without guilt.
Mary was cleansed from sin by the Spirit and was free of all sin.
Christ did not descend from Abraham by seminal reason through concupiscence.
Christ took the likeness of sinful flesh, sharing our penalty but not our guilt.
The Word was united to soul and flesh at conception.

pl-l3d4.summary: Asks why Scripture attributes the incarnation, a work of the whole Trinity, to the Spirit: because he is the charity and gift of God, and naming one person implies all three (c1). Christ is born of the Spirit but is not his son, since not everything born of something is its son. His birth from the Spirit signifies the grace by which, without merit, a man was joined to the Word, and the Spirit was the efficient cause, not the seed, of his conception (c2). Paul says Christ was 'made', not 'born', of a woman because he was formed by the Spirit's power without seed, yet 'of the seed of David' because his mother's flesh came from seed (c3).
claims: The incarnation is appropriated to the Spirit as charity and gift.
Christ is born of the Spirit but is not the Spirit's son.
The Spirit is the efficient cause, not the seed, of Christ's conception.
Christ's birth from the Spirit signifies the grace of union.

pl-l3d5.summary: Asks what assumed what. It is certain that the person of the Word assumed a nature and that no person was assumed. Whether nature assumed nature is disputed: the Councils of Toledo seem to deny it, but Augustine, Hilary, and Jerome (on the form of God taking the form of a servant) affirm it. Lombard harmonizes: the divine nature united human nature to itself in the Son's person, so it is truly incarnate, and 'only the Son' excludes the other persons, not the divine nature (c1). The divine nature should not be called 'made flesh', lest conversion be suggested, nor properly 'man', since it did not take man into its own singularity, though some grant both (c2). The Word did not assume a human person: soul and flesh were not a person before union, a soul united to another is not a person, and 'the man was assumed' refers to the nature (c3).
claims: The person of the Word assumed human nature, not a human person.
The divine nature assumed human nature in the person of the Son and is truly incarnate.
The divine nature should not be called 'made flesh' or properly 'man'.
A soul united to another is not a person.
'The man was assumed' refers to the nature.

pl-l3d6.summary: Raises the central question of how 'God was made man' and 'God is man' are to be understood, on which the wise differ (c1), and sets out three opinions with their authorities. The first holds that a man of soul and flesh began to be God by grace in the person of the Word (c2). The second holds that the Word's person, simple before, became composite of two natures or three substances, the person of God becoming also the person of a man (c3). The third holds that soul and flesh were united to the Word like a garment, no new substance being formed, so that God is man by habitus, by having a man (c4). Augustine's account of habitus, especially the garment shaped by the wearer, supports the third (c5–c6).
claims: Lombard sets out three opinions on how God became man.
First opinion: a man of soul and flesh began to be God by grace.
Second opinion: the Word's person became composite of two natures.
Third opinion: the Word put on soul and flesh like a garment, being man by habitus.

pl-l3d7.summary: Explains how each of the three opinions understands 'God was made man' and 'Christ as man is predestined', and answers objections. The first accepts that a substance which was not always God is God, with further objections left to the reader. The second reads 'God is man' as predicating the person or the divine nature (c1). The second also reads texts about the assumed man as about the nature, and texts about 'one thing and another' as about two natures, the union not being of parts. The third, which the authorities hardly oppose, reads 'God is man' as God having a man, and Christ as less than the Father by habitus: God made man, not man deified (c2). 'Lordly man' is not to be said. Lombard ends without asserting any opinion, holding firmly that God assumed man without change of either nature (c3).
claims: The first opinion accepts that a substance that was not always God is God.
On the second opinion, the union is not of parts in a whole.
On the third opinion, God is man by having a man.
God was made man; man was not deified.
Lombard presents the opinions without asserting one.
God assumed man without change of either nature.

pl-l3d8.summary: Asks whether the divine nature is born of the Virgin. Since it is not born of the Father, it should not be called born of the mother; Augustine's text about the eternal nature being born refers to the person (c1). Christ was born twice, once from the Father before the ages and once from his mother in time, both births belonging to the one Son (c2).
claims: The divine nature is not born of the Virgin.
The person of the Son is born of the Father and of the mother.
Christ has two births.

pl-l3d9.summary: Asks whether Christ's humanity is adored with latria, owed to God alone. Some say it receives a special dulia; others that it is adored with one adoration with the Word, as united to him and for his sake, which is not idolatry. Damascene's coal, Augustine's royal purple, and the footstool of Ps 98 settle the question for one adoration (c1).
claims: Latria is owed to God alone.
Christ's humanity is adored with the Word in one adoration.
Adoring Christ's humanity as united to the Word is not idolatry.

pl-l3d10.summary: Asks whether Christ as man is a person or something. The phrase 'according as' can signify nature, unity of person, habitus, or cause; Christ's soul is a rational substance but not a person; Christ is predestined as man to be Son of God by grace but is not Son of God by being man (c1). Christ is in no way an adopted son but Son by nature; he is son of the Virgin by nature and by the grace of union, not of adoption (c2). Both the person, according to the assumed humanity, and the human nature were predestined (c3).
claims: 'According as man' must be distinguished.
Christ's soul is not a person.
Christ is not an adopted son.
Christ is son of the Virgin by grace of union, not adoption.
Both person and nature were predestined.

pl-l3d11.summary: Asks whether Christ should be called made or a creature. Simply, no: the Son, through whom all things were made, is not made (Augustine, Ambrose) (c1). Arius held Christ a creature; Christ may be called made only with a qualification, 'according to the flesh', since being made belongs to the humanity, and no argument may proceed from such figurative statements (c2). That man began as man and always was as Word: regarding the person he always was, regarding the nature he began (c3).
claims: Christ is not simply a creature.
Christ is made only according to the flesh.
One cannot argue validly from figurative statements.
As person Christ always was; as to human nature he began.

pl-l3d12.summary: Considers what God could have done. He could have assumed another soul and flesh, even from outside Adam's race, but it was more fitting to take a man from the conquered race, conceived without concupiscence (c1). As person Christ could neither sin nor not be God; his soul united to the Word could not sin, though it could if not united, as confirmed angels have free choice yet cannot sin (c2). God could perhaps have assumed the female sex, but assuming a man born of a woman showed the liberation of both sexes (c3).
claims: God could have assumed another man or one from outside Adam's race.
Christ, as person and in his united soul, could not sin.
Free choice does not imply the ability to sin.
Assuming a man born of a woman showed the liberation of both sexes.

pl-l3d13.summary: Teaches that Christ as man had the fullness of grace and wisdom from conception, as the head has all the senses while members have only touch; the saints receive a like grace. He advanced in wisdom and grace in others, by revealing it, not in himself. Following a careful reading of Ambrose, Christ has two wisdoms, uncreated and created, in one person; his apparent progress and childhood ignorance refer to appearance (c1).
claims: Christ had the fullness of grace and wisdom from conception.
The saints receive from Christ's fullness a like grace.
Christ advanced in others, not in himself.
Christ has uncreated and created wisdom in one person.

pl-l3d14.summary: Holds that Christ's soul knows all that God knows, in the Word, against those who say no creature can equal the Creator in knowledge; but it knows less clearly than God and so is not equal to him, and it cannot do all God can. Since the Spirit was given to it without measure, its knowledge has no measure (c1). It received knowledge, of which it is naturally capable, but not omnipotence, lest it be thought God; Ambrose's statement that the man received in time the Son's power refers to the person as person of a man (c2).
claims: Christ's soul knows all that God knows, in the Word.
Christ's soul knows less clearly than God and is not equal to him.
Christ's soul was not given omnipotence.
The person received in time, as man, the power it always had as God.
concepts: person of God and person of man

pl-l3d15.summary: Teaches that Christ assumed a passible soul and flesh with defects of penalty but not of guilt, only those fitting for him and useful to us: not ignorance or difficulty in doing good. He took them by will of mercy, not by necessity, and truly felt pain, fear, and sorrow (c1). Authorities that seem to deny his fear and sorrow deny only passio and necessity: his affections were propassio, never moving his mind from rectitude (c2). Hilary's words that Christ felt no pain mean he had no cause or merit of pain in himself (c3), and Hilary affirms that Christ was sorrowful for his disciples and that the Word suffered without being changed (c4).
claims: Christ assumed defects of penalty, not guilt, and only fitting ones.
Christ did not take ignorance or difficulty in doing good.
Christ took his defects by will, not necessity.
Christ truly felt pain, fear, and sorrow, but as propassio.
Hilary's apparent denial of Christ's pain means he had no cause of pain in himself.

pl-l3d16.summary: Teaches that Christ had the aptitude for dying, which is no defect, and took the necessity of suffering and dying by will, not by his sinless condition; it is called natural as a defect of fallen nature (c1). Christ took something from each of man's four states: sinlessness from the state before sin, penalty from the fallen state, fullness of grace from the state of grace, and impeccability and contemplation of God from glory (c2).
claims: Christ took the necessity of dying by will.
The necessity of dying is a defect of fallen nature.
Christ took something from each of man's four states.

pl-l3d17.summary: Asks whether Christ willed or prayed for what did not happen (c1). Christ had two wills, divine and human; by the will of reason he willed to die, by the will of sensuality he shrank from death, without any conflict of flesh against spirit. Bede, Jerome, Augustine, and Ambrose confirm two wills against those who deny it. He prayed by sensuality for what he did not obtain, to teach his members to submit their wills (c2). Ambrose's 'as man he doubts' means he acted as one doubting; Hilary holds that Christ prayed for his disciples, not himself, words to be read with care (c3).
claims: Christ had two wills, divine and human.
By reason Christ willed to die; by sensuality he shrank from death.
There was no conflict of flesh against spirit in Christ.
Christ's prayer gives an example of submission.
Christ did not doubt but acted as one doubting.
concepts: will of reason and of sensuality

pl-l3d18.summary: Treats Christ's merit. He merited for his members redemption and the opening of the kingdom, and for himself the glory of impassibility and immortality, by humble obedience (c1). He merited as much from conception through his virtues as later through his passion, increasing merits in number but not force, and could not become better (c2). He merited not the name above every name, which he had by nature and grace, but its manifestation after the resurrection (c3). As passible man he could not reach glory without merit, though he could have without the merit of the passion (c4). He suffered for us, as form and cause of our salvation: God decreed that only a humility sufficient for all could open paradise, and Christ's humility, exceeding Adam's pride, did so (c5).
claims: Christ merited for himself and for his members.
Christ merited from conception as much as by his passion.
Christ merited the manifestation of his name, not the name itself.
Christ suffered for us, as form and cause of our salvation.
Only Christ's humility was sufficient to open paradise.

pl-l3d19.summary: Explains how Christ's death redeems us. Freed from sin, we are freed from the devil. His death justifies us by kindling our love through God's love shown in it, and through faith in his passion; the devil, who killed the sinless one, lost his debtors (c1). A man had to conquer the devil, and God had to be in him to keep him sinless (c2). Christ frees us from eternal penalty now and from temporal penalty in the future (c3), and his penalty remits temporal penalty in baptism and lessens it in penance (c4). The Son is properly redeemer, by power as God and by humility as man (c5). He alone is mediator, since God loved us before reconciliation and the Trinity reconciles by power, the Son alone by obedience (c6). He is mediator according to his humanity, between men and the Trinity (c7).
claims: Christ's death justifies us by kindling love and through faith.
By killing the sinless Christ, the devil lost his hold on believers.
Christ's penalty remits temporal penalty in baptism and lessens it in penance.
The Son is properly redeemer and alone mediator.
Christ is mediator according to his humanity.

pl-l3d20.summary: Asks whether God could free man otherwise than by Christ's death: he could, but no way was more fitting (c1). God willed to conquer the devil by justice, not power; man was given to the devil by just permission (c2). Killing the sinless Christ cost the devil his claim, and God chose justice so that men would imitate it, though power alone could have freed man justly (c3–c4). Christ is priest, victim, and price, offered to the Trinity, sufficient for all and effective for the elect; the Father, Christ, Judas, and the Jews all handed him over with different wills, different acts in one thing done (c5). The passion is the work of God and of the Jews, who worked good in the result and evil in their action (c6).
claims: God could have freed man otherwise, but Christ's death was most fitting.
God conquered the devil by justice, not power.
Christ is priest, victim, and price, sufficient for all and effective for the elect.
One thing done, the passion, involved good and evil acts according to intention.

pl-l3d21.summary: Asks whether, in Christ's death, the soul or the flesh was separated from the Word. Lombard rejects the view, argued from the soul's mediation and from Ambrose and Athanasius, that the divinity left the flesh: the divinity withdrew its protection, not the union, and Athanasius' 'assumed anew' refers to the reuniting of soul and body at the resurrection. In death soul was parted from flesh, but neither from the Word, and Christ laid down his life by his own power (c1). God is therefore said to have died and suffered because the flesh and soul united to him died and suffered, while the divinity felt no pain; he died and did not die, suffered and did not suffer, according to one nature or the other (c2).
claims: In Christ's death neither soul nor flesh was separated from the Word.
The divinity's 'forsaking' of Christ was a withdrawal of protection, not of union.
Christ laid down his soul by his own power.
God is said to die and suffer because of the flesh and soul united to him.
The divinity felt no pain.

pl-l3d22.summary: Asks whether Christ was a man during the three days of death. He was truly man though neither mortal nor immortal, since the mystery of faith is free from dialectical subtleties; he was man by the union of soul and flesh with himself and dead by their separation from each other (c1). He was not man wherever he is, but was man in the tomb by the flesh and in hell by the soul, keeping one and the same union with both though they were separated (c2). He was whole (totus) at once in tomb, hell, heaven, and everywhere, but not the whole (totum), since 'totum' refers to nature and 'totus' to hypostasis (c3). Exchanged predicates such as 'the son of man descended from heaven' hold by unity of person, not distinction of natures; Lombard then closes the treatment of the incarnation, enough said about the strap of the Lord's sandal (c4).
claims: Christ was truly man in death, neither mortal nor immortal.
In death Christ was man by union with soul and flesh, dead by their separation.
Christ kept one union with soul in hell and flesh in the tomb.
Christ was totus but not totum in each place.
Exchanged predicates hold by unity of person, not distinction of natures.

pl-l3d23.summary: Lombard opens the treatise on the theological virtues by asking whether Christ, full of grace, also had faith and hope, and answers by first giving a full account of faith. Faith is the virtue by which unseen things pertaining to religion are believed. 'Faith' is said in three ways: formed faith (a virtue, informed by charity), unformed faith (a real quality of mind and gift of God, but no virtue, which demons and bad Christians have), and the content believed. Using Augustine's triad, he separates believing God exists and believing God's word, which the wicked can do, from believing into God, which loves and adheres to him and justifies. When charity comes, the unformed quality probably remains and becomes a virtue. Faith is one in content for all but one only in kind as a habit. It properly concerns only the non-apparent, yet is seen intellectually by its possessor. Expounding Hebrews 11:1, faith is the substance and foundation of hoped-for goods and the proof of unseen things. The act of faith naturally precedes hope and charity, though charity, being the Holy Spirit and mother of the virtues, is the cause of faith as a virtue, not its effect. To believe is to think with assent.
claims: Faith is the virtue by which unseen things pertaining to religion are believed.
Faith is said as formed virtue, as unformed quality, and as content believed.
Only believing into God, which includes love and adherence, justifies; believing that God exists or that his word is true is shared by the wicked.
Unformed faith is a real quality and gift of God which likely becomes a virtue when charity arrives.
Faith is numerically one as content, but one only by likeness as a habit.
Faith properly concerns only the non-apparent, though it is itself known intellectually by its possessor.
Faith is the foundation of all virtues and good works, but not of charity, which causes it.
The act of faith naturally, not temporally or causally, precedes the acts of hope and charity.

pl-l3d24.summary: Lombard defends and refines the thesis that faith concerns only what is unseen. Against John 14:29 he argues with Augustine that seen things only prompt belief in unseen things, as Thomas saw flesh and believed God; ordinary talk of believing one's eyes is improper, and the heavenly 'faith of things' is not faith but its reward. Peter's faith in the passion lay not in believing that a man suffered, which he saw, but that God suffered; the merit of faith lies in believing the God-man died. Finally, faith is not about the wholly unknown: it is not of objects of bodily sight but can concern what interior vision grasps. Some things must be understood to be believed, others believed to be understood; faith comes from hearing, purifies the heart, and increases understanding, so that what is believed is partly but not wholly unknown, as one can love what one does not fully know. Perfect knowledge of God awaits the next life.
claims: Faith properly concerns only the unseen; visible things merely occasion belief in invisible ones.
The beatific 'faith of things' is not properly faith but its reward.
Faith in the passion consists in believing that the one who suffered is God.
Faith concerns objects of interior, not exterior, vision and is never about the wholly unknown.
Some truths must be understood before belief, others believed before understanding.
Faith purifies the heart and increases understanding, while perfect knowledge awaits the next life.

pl-l3d25.summary: Lombard turns to the sufficiency of faith for salvation across history. Faith has grown over time in knowledge and articles, and while Hebrews 11:6 (believing that God exists and rewards) is a necessary minimum, it never sufficed: from Adam's fall onward no one has been saved without faith in the Mediator, the ancients believing in future what we believe as past. Not everyone needed explicit knowledge: revelation was distinct for the greater (Abraham, Moses) and veiled for the simple, who believed implicitly by adhering to the greater, as less capable Christians now hold the Creed. Lombard reports, without deciding between them, opinions on the minimum the ancients had to believe about Christ (four articles, or the Son's birth and judgment given faith in the Trinity). He resolves the case of Cornelius, who believed in the incarnation without knowing it had occurred, with Peter sent to announce it and baptize. He closes by holding with Gregory that faith, hope, charity, and works are equal in intensity in this life, while charity is greater because it endures and mothers the virtues; it is said to 'proceed' from faith and hope only because it never exists without them.
claims: Belief that God exists and rewards is necessary but never sufficient for salvation.
No one before or after Christ has been saved without faith in the Mediator.
The ancients and moderns share one faith differing only in tense.
Revelation may be distinct (explicit) or veiled (implicit); the simple are saved by implicit faith adhering to the greater.
Cornelius had faith in the incarnation without knowing it had been fulfilled.
Faith, hope, charity, and works are equal in intensity in this life, but charity is greater.
Charity does not arise from faith and hope but presupposes them.

pl-l3d26.summary: Defines hope as the certain expectation of future beatitude from grace and preceding merits; hoping without merits is presumption (c1). Like faith, hope concerns the unseen (c2), but faith extends to good and bad, past, present, and future, one's own and others', while hope regards only future goods pertaining to the hoper (c3). Returning to the question that opened the treatise, Lombard reports, approvingly, that Christ had no virtues of faith and hope, since like the blessed and angels he knew clearly what he believed and hoped (c4), while the ancient fathers in hell had faith and hope until the passion opened vision (c5).
claims: Hope is the certain expectation of beatitude from grace and merits.
Faith has a broader object than hope.
Christ did not have the virtues of faith and hope, seeing clearly what he believed.
The ancient fathers in hell had faith and hope.

pl-l3d27.summary: Christ, who lacked faith and hope, had the greatest charity, shown in his death for friends and enemies (c1). Charity is love of God for himself and neighbor for God, with two commandments on which the Law hangs (c2). One and the same charity, the Holy Spirit, loves God and neighbor (c3); it is called twofold only because of its two objects (c4). Neighbor is loved as oneself, in the good and for God, and every man is neighbor; one who loves iniquity hates himself; God is loved with heart, soul, and mind, that is, intellect, will, and memory (c5). The commandment of total love is fulfilled only in part here and wholly in the homeland; it is given to show the goal of the race (c6). Each commandment implies the other (c7). Only rational creatures in fellowship with us and our body are to be loved with charity (c8).
claims: Christ had the greatest possible charity.
One charity, the Holy Spirit, loves God and neighbor.
Neighbor is loved for God and in the good; every man is a neighbor.
The commandment of total love is fulfilled in part here and wholly in the homeland.
Love of God and love of neighbor imply each other.

pl-l3d28.summary: Every kind of thing to be loved is contained in the two commandments: of Augustine's four objects, God, self, neighbor, and body, love of self and body needs no separate commandment, being natural and contained in 'as yourself' (c1). The question whether angels belong to the neighbor-commandment (c2) is answered that every man, including enemies, is neighbor, and since 'neighbor' is relative, the angels who show us mercy are included; God is not, being loved above ourselves, while Christ as man is loved more than ourselves but less than God (c3). 'Neighbor' is said in four ways (c4).
claims: The two commandments contain every object of love.
Self-love and love of one's body are natural and included in neighbor-love.
Every man, including enemies, and the holy angels are neighbors.
God is to be loved above ourselves; Christ as man more than ourselves but less than God.

pl-l3d29.summary: Treats the order of charity. Rightly ordered love loves God above all and oneself, and another man's soul above one's body (c1). On whether all men are loved equally, Lombard sets out the view that affection is equal and only services differ, against the commandment to honor parents, Jerome, and Ambrose, and favors, as not unlearned, an order in affection as well as in effect: God, self, parents, children and siblings, household, enemies. Augustine's 'equality' concerns the good wished. Whether good strangers are loved more than wicked kin is left an obscure question; enemies are loved as ourselves though less than other neighbors, and in all we love nature and hate vice (c2). Charity has degrees, beginning, advancing, perfect, most perfect, and its perfection is readiness to die for others (c3).
claims: Charity is ordered: God above all, then self, then neighbors in order.
The order of charity holds in affection as well as in services.
Augustine's 'equal love' refers to the good wished.
Enemies are to be loved as ourselves, though less than other neighbors.
Charity has degrees, perfected in readiness to die for others.

pl-l3d30.summary: Asks whether it is more meritorious to love friends or enemies. Loving both is better than loving friends alone, while within one person the comparison is obscure. Augustine seems to say loving enemies is greater and belongs to the perfect, and that many fulfil the Lord's Prayer by forgiving without loving enemies; since sins are not forgiven without charity, this would allow charity without love of enemies. Rejecting the view that love of enemies is a precept only for the perfect, Lombard holds that all are commanded to love enemies, and reads Augustine as speaking of their perfect love.
claims: Loving friends and enemies is better than loving friends alone.
All are commanded to love their enemies.
Perfect love of enemies belongs to the perfect.

pl-l3d31.summary: Rejects the view that charity once had cannot be lost and that the damned never had it, a view supported by many authorities. Some are good for a time and then bad, and names are written in the book of life by present justice; the authorities concern charity's permanence in the future, its efficacy, final perseverance, or perfect charity, which cannot be lost, while beginning charity can be, though while present it excludes mortal sin (c1). Charity, unlike faith and hope, is not done away in the homeland but loses only its imperfection; knowledge remains with another mode (c2). Christ as man loved with the charity of the homeland, wishing salvation only for the elect, as the blessed will only what God wills (c3).
claims: Charity once had can be lost, except perfect charity.
While charity is present it excludes mortal sin.
In the homeland charity remains, faith and hope cease, and knowledge changes mode.
Christ loved with the charity of the homeland, willing the salvation of the elect.

pl-l3d32.summary: Treats God's love for us, which is the divine essence and the same love by which we love him. God loves all he made, rational creatures more, the members of his Son more, and the Son most (c1). His love is immutable, so 'more' and 'less' mean that he wills greater or lesser goods to some (c2): his love varies by efficacy, not essence, and those justified 'begin to be loved' in that they receive its effect; they change, not God (c3). One may be loved more at one time than another by effect, not essence (c4). Of the reprobate it is to be said simply that God hated, that is, reprobated them, and loved them only as his future work (c5).
claims: God's love is the divine essence and is immutable.
God loves all he made, in degrees.
God's greater or lesser love means greater or lesser goods willed.
God's love varies by efficacy, not essence.
God loved the reprobate only as his work.

pl-l3d33.summary: Introduces the cardinal virtues, justice, fortitude, prudence, and temperance, by which one lives well here and reaches eternal life (c1). They were most fully in Christ, with the uses of the homeland and some of the way (c2). Following Augustine and Bede, they will remain in the homeland: justice as subjection to God, the others without error, trouble, or struggle, though their present works will cease (c3).
claims: There are four cardinal virtues.
The cardinal virtues were fully in Christ.
The cardinal virtues remain in the homeland with other uses.

pl-l3d34.summary: Treats the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: whether they are virtues, whether they remain in the future, and whether they were in Christ (c1). Ambrose shows they are virtues, abounding in the angels, so they remain (c2); Isaiah shows they were in Christ. Bede and Augustine say all fear will cease, but this concerns its present use: in the homeland filial fear becomes reverence, love mixed with subjection, which Christ also had (c3). Lombard distinguishes four fears, worldly, servile, initial, and chaste (c4), expounds Augustine on how perfect charity casts out fear while chaste fear endures (c5), and with the image of two wives distinguishes servile fear of punishment from chaste fear of separation, placing initial fear between them, in beginning charity (c6). Both servile and initial fear are called the beginning of wisdom for different reasons (c7). Fear remains in the future as reverence and was in Christ in that form (c8); his fear of penalty was natural fear, an effect of sin (c9).
claims: The seven gifts are virtues and remain in the homeland with changed uses.
The gifts were in Christ.
There are four fears: worldly, servile, initial, and chaste.
Perfect charity casts out servile fear; chaste fear endures as reverence.
Christ had fear as reverence and natural fear of penalty, but not servile or initial fear.

pl-l3d35.summary: Distinguishes three gifts. Wisdom concerns divine things and contemplation, knowledge human things and action, limited to what serves saving faith; Christ, God and man, is the object of both (c1). Understanding concerns the Creator and invisible creatures, while wisdom regards eternal Truth alone and delights in it (c2). These gifts are infused virtues that reform and help natural understanding and reason darkened by sin; the wisdom given is human wisdom by participation in God's light (c3).
claims: Wisdom concerns divine things, knowledge human things.
Understanding concerns the Creator and invisible creatures; wisdom delights in eternal Truth.
The gifts are infused virtues that heal natural powers.
The gift of wisdom is a participation in God.

pl-l3d36.summary: Holds with Jerome and Augustine that the virtues are connected, since charity is their mother (c1). On whether they are equal, Lombard prefers that all virtues are together and equal in habit, while one may exercise one more than another, or not at all, in act; pre-eminence in a virtue refers to outward acts, and sins are unequal according as they oppose charity (c2). All the Law's precepts, the moral ones and the ceremonial ones in their spiritual sense, are referred through the Decalogue to the two commandments of charity, its fullness and end; the ceremonial ones ceased as shadows (c3).
claims: The virtues are connected through charity.
The virtues are equal in habit, though not in act.
Sins are unequal according to their opposition to charity.
All precepts are referred to the two commandments of charity.

pl-l3d37.summary: Turns to the Decalogue: three precepts on the first tablet concerning God, seven on the second concerning neighbor; Origen and Augustine count the first differently, and idol is distinguished from likeness (c1). The idol's form is not from God as idol; the second precept forbids vain oaths and, allegorically, thinking Christ a creature; the third commands the Sabbath and, allegorically, rest from the Spirit (c2). The three first-tablet precepts correspond to Father, Son, and Spirit; the second tablet begins with honoring parents and forbids killing in deed and will (c3). Adultery covers every illicit union and theft every unjust taking, including sacrilege and usury (c4). The Israelites who despoiled the Egyptians at God's command did not sin, and the golden rule means 'unjustly'; false witness forbids lying and perjury (c5). Whether every lie is forbidden is a great question (c6).
claims: The Decalogue has three precepts concerning God and seven concerning neighbor.
The first-tablet precepts correspond to the three persons.
The Gospel makes explicit the spiritual sense of the precepts.
Theft includes sacrilege and usury.
Acting at God's command, the Israelites did not steal.

pl-l3d38.summary: Treats lying. There are three kinds of lies, helpful, jesting, and malicious; the first two are venial for the imperfect, but the perfect should not lie even to save a life, though they may keep silent (c1). Augustine's eight kinds of lies range from the capital lie in religious teaching downward; none is without sin (c2).
