A lie is a false signification with intent to deceive (c3), while lying is speaking against one's mind, so that one may lie while saying something true and not lie while saying something false (c4). Every lie is a sin, its gravity depending on intent and subject, because words are instituted to express thought; yet not every lie is mortal or forbidden by the commandment (c5). Error in matters irrelevant to salvation is slight or no sin, and Jacob's claim to be Esau was a mystery, not a lie (c6).
claims: There are three, or by Augustine eight, kinds of lies of differing gravity.
A lie is a false signification with intent to deceive.
Lying is speaking against one's mind, and one can lie while saying something true.
Every lie is a sin, since speech is for expressing thought.
The perfect should not lie even to save a life.
Jacob's deception was a mystery, not a lie.

pl-l3d39.summary: Treats perjury, a lie confirmed by oath. Some hold that swearing falsely without a lie is perjury, others not (c1–c2); Lombard holds that one perjures by swearing falsely knowingly, rashly, or by swearing truly against one's mind, and that a sworn promise becomes perjury when broken (c3). Swearing from necessity is not evil; Christ forbade swearing from desire (c4). The Jews were forbidden to swear by creatures, lest they worship them (c5); oaths by God bind most (c6); every oath calls God as witness or pledges something to him (c7). One may use the faith of one who swore by false gods (c8). Oaths against faith and charity should be broken, as David's against Nabal (c9), and the guilt lies in having sworn them (c10). God takes an oath as the hearer understands it (c11), and compelling a known false oath is worse than murder (c12).
claims: Perjury includes false, rash, and insincere swearing.
Necessary oaths are lawful; swearing from desire is forbidden.
Every oath calls God as witness or pledges something to God.
Unjust oaths should be broken; the guilt lies in swearing them.
Compelling a known false oath is worse than murder.

pl-l3d40.summary: Completes the Decalogue: the last two precepts forbid coveting the neighbor's wife and goods, differing from those against adultery and theft as desire from deed; the Law is said to restrain only the hand in its ceremonial precepts (c1). The 'letter that kills' is the Decalogue, good in itself but deadly without grace, since it increases concupiscence (c2). The Law and Gospel differ in promises, sacraments, and ceremonial precepts, but share the moral precepts, more fully in the Gospel; Book 3 closes with the ten strings of the psaltery, to be plucked with charity (c3).
claims: The last two precepts forbid desire, not deeds.
The Law is good but kills without grace.
The Gospel promises heavenly goods and its sacraments confer grace.
The moral precepts are the same in Law and Gospel.

pl-liber3.summary: Summary of Book 3 (on the incarnation, the virtues, and the commandments), based on the prologue and all 40 distinctions. The prologue places Books 3 and 4 as the restoration of fallen man through the grace of the Mediator and the sacraments, as the Samaritan comes to the wounded man. Distinctions 1 to 5 present the incarnation as the Son's mission: only the Son became incarnate, though the whole Trinity worked it; he assumed whole human nature, soul and flesh, at conception, through the soul's mediation, sanctified by the Spirit, and the Word assumed a human nature but not a human person. Distinctions 6 and 7 set out three opinions on how God became man without deciding among them. Distinctions 8 to 12 treat Christ's two births, the adoration of his humanity, his natural sonship, the qualified sense in which he is a creature, and his impeccability. Distinctions 13 to 17 treat his fullness of grace and wisdom, his soul's knowledge, his voluntary defects of penalty, his propassio, and his two wills. Distinctions 18 to 20 treat his merit, redemption from sin, the devil, and penalty through his death, his mediation according to his humanity, and the devil's defeat by justice rather than power. Distinctions 21 and 22 hold that in death neither soul nor flesh was parted from the Word, that God died and suffered in the flesh, and that Christ was man in the tomb and in hell, whole everywhere but not the whole, closing the treatment of the incarnation. Distinctions 23 to 26 treat faith, formed and unformed, its object, its relation to understanding, its necessity in every age, and hope, holding that Christ, seeing clearly, had neither faith nor hope as virtues. Distinctions 27 to 32 treat charity: one charity, the Holy Spirit, loves God and neighbor; its mode, objects, and order, which Lombard holds applies to affection as well as service; love of enemies, commanded to all; its degrees and its loss, except when perfect; and God's own immutable love, varying only in its effects. Distinctions 33 to 36 treat the cardinal virtues and the seven gifts, which remain in the homeland with changed uses, the four kinds of fear, wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, and the connection and equality of the virtues in charity. Distinctions 37 to 40 expound the Decalogue as fulfilled in charity, with extended treatments of idolatry, theft and usury, lying, and perjury and oaths, and close with the contrast between the killing letter of the Law and the grace of the Gospel.
claims: Books 3 and 4 treat restoration through the Mediator's grace and the sacraments.
Only the Son became incarnate, though the whole Trinity worked the incarnation.
The Word assumed whole human nature, soul and flesh, at conception, but not a human person.
Lombard reports three opinions on the union without deciding among them.
Christ had fullness of grace from conception, two wisdoms, and two wills.
Christ merited for himself and for us; his death redeems from sin, the devil, and penalty.
In death neither soul nor flesh was separated from the Word.
Faith formed by charity, explicit or implicit, is necessary for salvation.
Christ had charity but not the virtues of faith and hope.
One charity, the Holy Spirit, loves God and neighbor, and is ordered in affection.
The virtues are connected and equal in habit through charity.
The Decalogue is fulfilled in the two commandments of charity.
Every lie is a sin, and perjury includes rash and insincere swearing.

pl-l4d1.summary: Opens the doctrine of signs with the Samaritan binding the wounded man: God instituted the sacraments as remedies against original and actual sin (c1). A sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing and the visible form of invisible grace (c2); a sign brings something else to mind (c3). Every sacrament is a sign but not conversely: a sacrament properly bears the likeness of grace and causes it, while the rites of the old law only signified and never justified (c4). Sacraments were instituted for humility, instruction, and exercise, though God did not bind his power to them, and they consist of words and things (c5). The old sacraments promised and signified, the new give salvation (c6), but circumcision remitted original and actual sin as baptism does, without opening heaven (c7); before it, others were justified by faith and sacrifices understood spiritually (c8). Circumcision was given to Abraham as a test of obedience and remedy for original sin, and was replaced by baptism, which also confers grace and virtues (c9). Infants who died before circumcision were lost, as unbaptized infants are (c10).
claims: God instituted the sacraments as remedies against sin.
A sacrament is a sign of a sacred thing that bears its likeness and causes it.
The legal rites signified but did not justify.
Sacraments were instituted for humility, instruction, and exercise, though God is not bound to them.
Circumcision remitted sin but did not confer grace or open heaven.

pl-l4d2.summary: Lists the seven sacraments of the new law, which differ in effect (remedy and grace, remedy only, or strengthening grace), and explains that they were given only after Christ, since they draw their power from his passion; marriage was instituted before sin (c1). Turning to baptism, the first sacrament, Lombard treats John's baptism: it washed bodies but did not remit sins, being unto repentance (c2–c3), prepared people for Christ's baptism and is called John's because only an outward human action occurred in it (c4), and was a sacrament only in the looser sense of the legal signs (c5). Those baptized by John who did not know the Holy Spirit later received Christ's baptism, while those who believed in the Trinity received the Spirit by the laying on of hands (c6).
claims: There are seven sacraments of the new law.
The sacraments draw their power from Christ's passion.
John's baptism was for repentance and did not remit sins.
Those baptized by John without knowing the Spirit received Christ's baptism.

pl-l4d3.summary: Defines baptism as an outward washing under the prescribed words; word and element are its substance, other rites its solemnity (c1). Its form is the invocation of the Trinity (c2); baptism in the name of Christ is valid, since the Trinity is understood in that name (c3); naming one person may suffice if the minister holds Trinitarian faith, though it is safer to name all three, 'in the name', not 'in the names' (c4). Baptism was most fittingly instituted at Christ's baptism in the Jordan, when his flesh gave water regenerative power (c5). It is performed only in water (c6), by single or triple immersion according to custom (c7). Circumcision lost its force at Christ's death (c8). The cause of baptism is the renewal of the mind, and its reality is justification; Christ's sacrifice, not baptism, opened heaven (c9).
claims: Baptism consists in word and element.
Its form is the invocation of the Trinity.
Baptism was instituted at Christ's baptism.
Only water is valid matter; immersion may be single or triple.
The reality of baptism is justification.

pl-l4d4.summary: Distinguishes those who receive the sacrament and its reality, the sacrament only, or the reality only. All baptized infants and faithful adults receive both, though only the elect to salvation (c1). Those who approach insincerely receive the sacrament without its reality, which begins to profit when they repent; Augustine's suggestion that sins are forgiven and return was tentative (c2). Putting on Christ can be sacramental or real (c3). Martyrdom, and faith and contrition where necessity rather than contempt excludes baptism, give its reality without the sacrament, since God is not bound to the sacraments; but unbaptized infants are not saved by the Church's faith (c4). Baptism gives those already justified release from outward satisfaction and increase of grace (c5), while temporal penalty remains for the sake of struggle (c6). The reality may precede or follow the sacrament, and some hold that infants receive grace as a gift, not yet in use (c7).
claims: Sacrament and reality may be received together or apart.
The insincere receive the sacrament only, until they repent.
Martyrdom and faith with contrition supply for baptism when necessity, not contempt, prevents it.
God is not bound to the sacraments.
Unbaptized infants are not saved.
Baptism increases grace and remits outward satisfaction in the already justified.

pl-l4d5.summary: Teaches that baptism given by good or bad ministers, even heretics or pagans, is equally true and holy, since it is God's gift, not man's; outside the Church it does not profit unto salvation, and it is never repeated (c1). Ministers have the ministry of baptism, not its power, which Christ kept for himself so that hope would not be placed in servants (c2). Asked what that power is, Lombard holds that God could have given a created, ministerial power to forgive sins, as he could create through a creature as minister, while modestly leaving room for a better explanation (c3).
claims: Baptism is equally valid whoever administers it.
Ministers have the ministry, not the power, of baptism.
Christ could have given a ministerial power to forgive sins but did not.
Baptism outside the Church does not profit unto salvation.

pl-l4d6.summary: Treats the minister, recipients, and rite of baptism. Priests baptize; deacons, laity, and women only in necessity (c1). Baptism given by heretics with the Church's form is valid and not repeated; Cyprian erred, but his martyrdom purged it (c2). Triple immersion is one baptism; no one is baptized in the womb, though Jeremiah and John were justified there beyond the common law (c3). Garbled words from ignorance do not invalidate, and those with no evidence of baptism should be baptized (c4). Baptism requires the intention to baptize, so baptism in jest is invalid; solemn baptism is at Easter and Pentecost (c5). Sponsors profess faith for infants, who 'believe' through the sacrament of faith and are bound by the promise (c6). Catechism and exorcism precede baptism as sacramentals, not as necessary for validity (c7).
claims: Priests baptize; others only in necessity.
Heretical baptism with the right form is valid and not repeated.
Baptism requires form and intention.
Infants believe through the sacrament of faith; sponsors promise for them.
Catechism and exorcism are sacramentals.

pl-l4d7.summary: Treats confirmation: its form is the bishop's words when anointing the forehead with chrism (c1); only bishops, successors of the apostles, can confer it (c2). Its power is the giving of the Spirit for strength, as baptism gives him for remission, so that the faithful become full Christians; Gregory's allowance for priests was a one-time concession (c3). It is held in greater veneration than baptism because of its ministers and place or its increase of virtues, though baptism avails more for remission, and it is given fasting (c4). Like baptism and orders, it is not repeated (c5).
claims: The form of confirmation is the bishop's words with chrismation.
Only bishops can confirm.
Confirmation gives the Spirit for strength.
Confirmation is not repeated.

pl-l4d8.summary: Introduces the eucharist, which perfects those cleansed by baptism and contains the source of all grace (c1). It was prefigured by the manna, by the blood and water from Christ's side, and by Melchizedek's bread and wine (c2). It was instituted at the Last Supper so that the sacrifice offered once might be continually honored (c3). Its form is Christ's words, at which bread and wine are converted into his body and blood (c4). It was given after supper to mark the end of the old sacraments and be remembered, but is received fasting (c5). The species of bread and wine are the sacrament (c6). Its reality is twofold: Christ's flesh and blood, contained and signified, and the unity of the Church, signified but not contained; so the species are sacrament only, Christ's body sacrament and reality, and the mystical body reality only (c7).
claims: The eucharist was instituted at the Last Supper.
Its form is Christ's words, at which bread and wine are converted.
Its reality is twofold: Christ's body and the Church's unity.
The species are sacrament only; Christ's body sacrament and reality; the Church's unity reality only.

pl-l4d9.summary: Distinguishes sacramental eating, common to good and bad, from spiritual eating, by which only the good remain in Christ and his Church; whoever believes eats, and a member of Christ shares in his body even without receiving the sacrament (c1). Against those who say the wicked do not receive Christ's body, Lombard holds that they receive it truly but only sacramentally, present in essence without saving efficacy, to their judgment (c2). He uses this distinction to interpret ambiguous sayings and liturgical prayers: Christ's body is received by good and bad, to salvation and to ruin (c3).
claims: Sacramental eating is common to good and bad; spiritual eating belongs only to the good.
Spiritual eating is remaining in Christ by faith and unity.
The wicked truly receive Christ's body, but without saving effect.

pl-l4d10.summary: Refutes those who, measuring God's power by nature, hold that Christ's body is on the altar only in sign. The texts they cite (John 6, Christ's body in one place, 'me you will not always have') deny only that his body is given torn apart or visibly; it is given whole and invisibly under bread and wine, visible in heaven and truly on every altar. Augustine's language of 'invisible flesh' uses a trope naming the sign by the thing signified (c1). Authorities from Christ, Ambrose, Augustine, and Eusebius prove that Christ's word, which created from nothing, can change substances, that after consecration bread and wine are his body and blood, and that the whole Christ is under each species, the substance of bread and wine being converted (c2).
claims: Some deny that Christ's body is on the altar except in sign.
Christ's body is present whole and invisibly under the species.
Christ is visible in heaven and truly on every altar.
Christ's word converts the substance of bread and wine into his body and blood.
The whole Christ is under each species.

pl-l4d11.summary: Lombard admits he cannot define the kind of conversion: it is not formal, since the species, taste, and weight remain; some hold it substantial, against the objection that Christ's body would then be increased daily (c1). The mystery is to be believed, not investigated; the bread is not matter of the body but is changed into it; of views that the bread is annihilated or that it remains alongside the body, he rejects the latter, holding that after consecration only the species of bread and wine remain (c2). Christ gave his body under another species so that faith would have merit and to avoid horror and mockery (c3), and under two species to signify the redemption of body and soul, though the whole Christ is under each, in one sacrament (c4). Water must be mixed with the wine, signifying the people united to Christ, though omission by ignorance does not invalidate; only wheat bread and wine may be used (c5). At the Supper Christ gave his then mortal body, and intinction should not be used (c6).
claims: The conversion is not formal; Lombard does not define it further.
After consecration only the species of bread and wine remain.
Christ's body is not increased by the conversion.
The whole Christ is under each species, in one sacrament.
Water mixed with wine signifies the people's union with Christ.

pl-l4d12.summary: The accidents of bread and wine remain without a subject, since Christ's body is not affected by them (c1). The breaking seen at the altar cannot be in Christ's incorruptible body; some say it is only apparent, others that it is a breaking in which nothing is broken (c2); Lombard holds it is a real breaking of the sacramental species, with Christ whole in each part, reading Berengar's confession accordingly (c3). The three parts of the host signify Christ risen, the Church on earth, and the dead, and the breaking represents the passion; one approaching in mortal sin receives unworthily (c4). What the priest offers is a sacrifice as memorial and representation of the cross, one victim offered once in itself and daily in the sacrament, remitting venial sins and perfecting virtue (c5). The eucharist was instituted to increase charity and heal daily weakness; Augustine neither praises nor blames daily communion, and the faithful should communicate at least three times a year (c6).
claims: The remaining accidents exist without a subject.
The breaking is real but occurs in the species, with Christ whole in each part.
The eucharist is a sacrifice as memorial and representation of the cross.
It remits venial sins, increases charity, and heals daily weakness.
Communion is required at least three times a year.

pl-l4d13.summary: Wicked priests within the Church validly consecrate, since the sacrament is effected by the Creator's word, not the minister's merit; but the excommunicated and manifest heretics seem unable to, since the priest offers in the person of the Church and the angel does not come to them. The eucharist requires form, priestly order, and intention, and one who misbelieves can still intend to do what others do; animals do not receive Christ's body, and contradicting this teaching is heresy (c1). A heretic is one who, for temporal gain, begets or follows false new opinions, heresy lying in the sense given to Scripture, not its words (c2).
claims: Wicked priests within the Church validly consecrate.
Excommunicated and heretical priests seem unable to consecrate.
The eucharist requires form, order, and intention.
Heresy lies in misunderstanding Scripture, chosen for temporal gain.

pl-l4d14.summary: Partial: rests on the four TEI chapters, which cover the EDF's five. Opens the treatise on penance, the second plank after shipwreck, which unlike baptism can be repeated and is both sacrament (outward) and virtue (inward) (c1). Penance is named from punishing and conceived by fear; against those who hold that true penance excludes later mortal sin, Lombard defines it as the virtue by which we lament and hate past evils with purpose of amendment, holds that later sin through weakness does not falsify it, and teaches that works done in charity revive through later penance (c2). 'One penance' refers to solemn public penance, granted once for notorious crimes (c3); penance itself can be repeated and pardon given again and again, as Augustine, Chrysostom, and David show (c4).
claims: Penance is both sacrament and virtue.
Penance is lamenting and hating past sins with purpose of amendment.
Later sin through weakness does not show that earlier penance was false.
Solemn penance is not repeated, but penance in general is.
Merits done in charity revive through penance.

pl-l4d15.summary: Refutes those who say one can repent of one sin while retaining another: 'God will not judge twice' applies only to those amended by punishment (c1), since scourges have five purposes, one the beginning of eternal punishment (c2). Gregory's partial rain concerns ceasing from a sin, not its pardon; Ambrose's 'even without faith' concerns unknown sins; satisfaction while retaining another sin is not true satisfaction, which consists in cutting off the causes of sin (c3). Forgiving offenses is the greatest alms, and alms must begin with mercy to one's own soul (c4–c5). So alms while persisting in mortal sin do not satisfy, and the hidden sin, once confessed, requires satisfaction for both; earlier works done in charity revive through penance (c6). Works without charity lessen punishment but do not merit life; one must repent of all sins, since half a pardon is impious; true penance hates sin and desires to satisfy, and requires restitution where possible (c7).
claims: One cannot repent of one sin while retaining another.
Satisfaction while persisting in sin is not satisfaction.
Alms do not purchase impunity.
Works without charity lessen punishment but do not merit life.
True penance requires restitution where possible.

pl-l4d16.summary: Perfect penance has three parts, contrition, confession, and satisfaction, answering the three ways of sinning and the three deaths (c1). Satisfaction must be proportioned to the fault, considering its circumstances, which must be confessed; the penitent submits wholly to the priest and must not divide his confession (c2). Penance is false when one persists in a sinful occupation, hatred, or unjust possession (c3). Penance is done before baptism, after baptism for grave sins, and daily for venial sins (c4), since accumulated small sins sink the soul like seeping water (c5). The Lord's Prayer with fasting and alms satisfies for venial sins; grave sins require more intense satisfaction (c6).
claims: Penance has three parts: contrition, confession, and satisfaction.
Satisfaction must be proportioned to the sin and its circumstances.
Penance is false while one persists in sin or unjust possession.
Venial sins are satisfied by the Lord's Prayer, fasting, and alms.

pl-l4d17.summary: Asks whether contrition alone remits sin, whether confession to God suffices, and whether confession to a layman avails. Lombard holds that sin is forgiven in contrition once one intends to confess, cleansing the stain and remitting eternal death, but that oral confession and satisfaction are still commanded if possible (c1). Against those who hold confession to God alone suffices (c2), he proves that confession must be made to priests, who hold the keys, in person, though not publicly for hidden sins (c3). Without a priest one should confess to a companion, the desire for a priest making one worthy of pardon; light sins may be confessed to equals (c4). The contrary authorities concern public penance; silence about sin comes from pride; confession is necessary even after contrition as punishment, as information for the priest, and for humility (c5).
claims: Sin is forgiven in contrition with the intention to confess.
Oral confession to a priest is required when possible.
Confessing to God alone does not suffice.
Without a priest one may confess to a layman.
Confession is part of punishment and makes the sinner humble.

pl-l4d18.summary: Asks what the priest forgives if contrition remits sin (c1). The keys are knowledge of discernment and power of binding and loosing, held only by the Church's true priests (c2–c3). Some hold that God cleanses the stain while the priest remits eternal death, but Lombard argues that God alone, in inspiring contrition, which requires charity, both cleanses and remits eternal death (c4), while still granting that priests have power to forgive and retain (c5). Priests bind and loose by declaring people bound or loosed, as priests judged lepers, by imposing and remitting satisfaction, and by excommunication (c6). Their sentence is ratified in heaven when it accords with merit; an unjust sentence harms only if despised (c7). The stain God removes is the soul's unlikeness to him, which priests, physicians of the living, cannot cure (c8).
claims: The keys are knowledge of discernment and power of binding and loosing.
God alone cleanses the soul and remits eternal death.
Priests bind and loose by declaring, imposing satisfaction, and excommunicating.
The priest's sentence is ratified in heaven when it accords with merit.
The stain of sin is the soul's unlikeness to God.

pl-l4d19.summary: Partial: rests on the three TEI chapters, which contain the EDF's four. The keys are given at priestly ordination; not all priests have the key of knowledge, but Lombard holds that all have the power of binding and loosing, though only those of apostolic life and doctrine use it worthily (c1). A bad priest still transmits grace by virtue of his order, as Caiaphas prophesied, while good priests bless lawfully and worthily (c2). Malachi's curse falls on heretics or on priests without knowledge and good life; the ecclesiastical judge must be free of what he judges, know how to discern and question, and may lose his power by falling (c3).
claims: The keys are given at ordination.
All priests have the power of the keys; only the worthy use it rightly.
A bad priest transmits grace by his order.
The ecclesiastical judge must be upright and knowledgeable.

pl-l4d20.summary: Penance is possible until the last moment of life, but deathbed penance gives no security, since it may come from fear rather than love; late penance is better than none, but one so converted must be purged by a purifying fire graver than any earthly pain (c1). Those who die with penance incomplete are freed if their contrition sufficed; otherwise they complete it in purgatorial fire, since God forgives by mercy but does not leave sin unpunished (c2). If imposed satisfaction was inadequate, sufficient inward grief still frees; priests should measure satisfaction by the grief of heart, and the canons leave this to their discretion (c3). Penance is made known, not imposed, to the dying (c4), and reconciliation must not be denied them (c5). Priests reconcile penitents only with the bishop's consent except in extreme need (c6), and offerings may be made for one who died seeking penance without a priest (c7).
claims: Penance is possible until death, but late penance is uncertain.
Incomplete penance is completed in purgatorial fire unless contrition sufficed.
God forgives by mercy but punishes by justice.
Priests should measure satisfaction by contrition.
Reconciliation must not be denied to the dying.

pl-l4d21.summary: Partial: rests on eight chapter files, which contain the EDF's nine. Some light sins are forgiven after this life, as Christ's words on the sin against the Spirit imply (c1). Those who build wood, hay, and straw, venial sins and lawful worldly attachments, are purged in a fire graver than any earthly pain (c2), longer or shorter as they loved perishable things more or less (c3); builders of gold, silver, and precious stones, the perfect, escape both fires, since charity consumes their venial sins (c4–c5). One can die in charity and true penance with unrepented venial sins, which are then purged, so sins themselves, not only their punishment, are forgiven hereafter (c6). Mortal sins must be confessed specifically, forgotten and venial ones generally, and general confession deletes unknown sins (c7). One must not confess sins not committed; a priest who reveals confessions is deposed; and a penitent may avoid an ignorant confessor but not despise his own priest (c8).
claims: Some light sins are forgiven after this life.
Venial sins and worldly attachments are purged by fire after death.
Mortal sins must be confessed specifically at least once.
A priest who reveals confessions is to be deposed.

pl-l4d22.summary: Asks whether forgiven sins return if one relapses or scorns confession: one view, citing the unforgiving servant, holds they return through ingratitude, and that this is not double punishment since unpersevering satisfaction was insufficient; another holds they are not punished again but ingratitude makes one as guilty. Lombard leaves the question to the reader (c1). In penance, some hold outward penance is the sacrament of inward contrition; others that outward penance is sacrament only, inward penance sacrament and reality, and remission of sins reality only (c2).
claims: Whether forgiven sins return is left undecided.
In penance, outward penance is sacrament, inward penance sacrament and reality, remission reality.

pl-l4d23.summary: Partial: rests on three of four chapter files; the third holds only a placeholder, its EDF chapter being contained in the second. The anointing of the sick is a sacrament given at the end with oil consecrated by the bishop (c1). There are three anointings, chrism, the oil of catechumens, and the oil of the sick; this sacrament was instituted by the apostles, as James shows, for remission of sins and relief of the body when expedient; its sacrament is the outward anointing, its reality the inward anointing of remission and increase of virtues, and contempt of it is damnable (c2). Unlike baptism, confirmation, and orders, it may be repeated; no sacrament's matter is consecrated twice, but some sacraments are received often (c4).
claims: The anointing of the sick is a sacrament instituted by the apostles.
It remits sins and relieves the body when expedient.
It may be repeated.

pl-l4d24.summary: Treats orders. There are seven grades, answering to the Spirit's sevenfold grace and all exercised by Christ: porter, lector, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, and priest (c1–c3); the tonsure signifies royal service and an open mind, and clerics are those allotted to the Lord (c4). Each grade is described with its Old Testament origin, duties, ordination rite, and Christ's exercise of it: porters keep the doors (c5), lectors read (c6), exorcists adjure spirits (c7), acolytes carry lights (c8), subdeacons serve at the altar and keep continence (c9), deacons assist in all sacraments and preach the Gospel (c10), and priests confect the eucharist, lacking only the episcopal powers of confirming (c11). Only the diaconate and priesthood are sacred orders in the eminent sense (c12). Order is a seal conferring spiritual power and grace (c13). Bishop, pontiff, patriarch, archbishop, and metropolitan name dignities and offices (c14–c17), and Lombard closes with vates and cantors, a call to ministers' holiness, and the meaning of 'Mass' (c18–c19).
claims: There are seven orders, answering to the sevenfold grace and exercised by Christ.
Only the diaconate and priesthood are sacred orders in the eminent sense.
Order is a seal conferring spiritual power and grace.
The episcopate is a dignity and office, not a separate order.
Ministers must excel in holiness as in dignity.

pl-l4d25.summary: Asks whether heretics can ordain and whether their ordinands must be reordained, on which authorities sharply disagree: some call heretical sacraments void and sacrilegious, while Augustine holds ordination, like baptism, remains and is not repeated. Lombard reports several resolutions, distinguishing heretics condemned by the Church, the form used, and validity from fruitfulness (c1). Simoniacs are heretics who validly ordain until degraded; those knowingly ordained by them are invalidly ordained, those unknowingly ordained tolerated; buying revenues is buying the spiritual; simony is threefold, with corresponding penalties; forced ordination may be excused (c2–c6). Canonical ages for ordination are fourteen, twenty-five, and thirty (c7).
claims: Authorities disagree on the validity of heretical ordinations.
Ordination, like baptism, is not repeated.
Simoniacs are heretics; knowing simoniacal ordination is void.
Canonical ages for ordination are fixed.

pl-l4d26.summary: Introduces marriage, instituted before sin as a duty and after sin as a remedy (c1–c2); the first institution was a precept, the second an indulgence (c3), marriage being a lesser good conceded and intercourse from incontinence a venial evil tolerated (c4). Against the Tatians, marriage is good, instituted by God and honored by Christ at Cana (c5). As a sacrament it signifies the union of Christ and the Church, consent signifying union by charity and carnal union union by nature; marriage without carnal union, like that of Mary and Joseph, is true and holy though it signifies only the union of charity (c6).
claims: Marriage was instituted before sin as duty and after as remedy.
Marriage is good, against the Tatians.
Marriage signifies the union of Christ and the Church.
Unconsummated marriage, like Mary and Joseph's, is true and holy.

pl-l4d27.summary: Defines marriage as the marital union of lawful persons in an undivided way of life (c1–c2). Its efficient cause is consent expressed in words of the present, not the future, and not intercourse (c3); spouses are such from a betrothal that expresses this consent, as Mary and Joseph were (c4). Against those who hold marriage begins only with carnal union, arguing that the betrothed may enter religion alone while spouses may not (c5–c8), Lombard distinguishes betrothal by future promise, which makes only betrothed persons free to enter religion, from betrothal by present consent, which makes true spouses (c8–c9). So a widow of a present-consent betrothal bars her later husband from orders, and a later union after present consent must yield to the first (c10).
claims: Marriage is the marital union of lawful persons in undivided life.
Present consent, not intercourse, makes marriage.
Betrothal by future promise differs from betrothal by present consent.
Spouses cannot enter religion without mutual consent.

pl-l4d28.summary: Sworn consent about the future does not make marriage; a later marriage stands and the perjury is corrected by penance, while after present consent a later union is void; the solemnities required by Evaristus concern marriage's dignity, not validity (c1). Present consent is the substance of marriage; secret marriage is valid but cannot be enforced without proof until publicly professed (c2). Marital consent is neither to cohabitation, else siblings could marry, nor to carnal union, given Mary's resolve of virginity (c3), but to conjugal society, as woman was formed from man's side as partner (c4).
claims: Sworn future promises do not make marriage.
Solemnities concern dignity, not validity.
Secret marriage is valid but unenforceable without proof.
Marital consent is consent to conjugal society.

pl-l4d29.summary: Marital consent must be free: forced consent does not make marriage, as Pope Urban ruled, though later free cohabitation without protest supplies consent; silence counts as consent and a daughter is presumed to consent to her father unless she dissents (c1).
claims: Forced consent does not make marriage.
Later free cohabitation supplies consent.

pl-l4d30.summary: Error of person and of servile condition void marriage, error of fortune or quality does not; Jacob's marriage to Leah was done in mystery, with consent following (c1). Mary and Joseph both intended virginity and consented to conjugal society, Mary to carnal union only at God's command; their marriage was perfect in holiness and in faith, offspring, and sacrament, bodily union perfecting marriage only as to signification (c2). Marriage's principal end is procreation, its second avoiding fornication, with other honorable and less honorable motives, which do not invalidate it (c3); a bad intention does not contaminate the sacrament, and Mary's marriage had special reasons (c4).
claims: Error of person or condition voids marriage.
Mary and Joseph's marriage was perfect in holiness and its three goods.
Procreation is the principal end of marriage.
Bad motives do not invalidate marriage.

pl-l4d31.summary: Sets out the three goods of marriage, faith, offspring, and sacrament (c1). Spouses may separate bodily for fornication or religion but not sacramentally, the bond remaining like baptism; the sacrament good signifies Christ's union with the Church; adultery or lack of offspring does not annul marriage, and the good of offspring is the desire to raise children religiously (c2). Those who procure sterility or abortion are fornicators, not spouses (c3), and abortion is homicide once the fetus is formed and ensouled (c4). With the goods, intercourse for offspring is without fault and intercourse from incontinence venial, while without faith and offspring it is not excused (c5); the Apostle's 'indulgence' permits the latter as a light fault (c6); the evil of incontinence becomes venial through the good of marriage, and rendering the debt is no sin (c7). Concupiscence is always an evil as a penalty of sin but not always a sin; Gregory's purity rule concerns intercourse not for offspring (c8).
claims: Marriage has three goods: faith, offspring, and sacrament.
The marriage bond is indissoluble while the spouses live.
Intercourse for offspring is without fault; from incontinence it is venial.
Abortion of a formed and ensouled fetus is homicide.
Concupiscence is a penalty of sin but not always a sin.

pl-l4d32.summary: Husband and wife are equal in the marital debt, neither having power over his own body; rendering it is no sin, demanding it beyond need venial (c1). Neither may vow continence without the other's consent, and a rash unilateral vow is to be corrected, not kept (c2). The debt must be rendered when asked but not sought on feasts, fasts, and processions, and ministers may not celebrate the mysteries after conjugal union (c3). Weddings are forbidden in Lent, Advent, and other seasons (c4).
claims: Spouses are equal in the marital debt.
Neither may vow continence without the other's consent.
Abstinence is required on holy days.
Weddings are forbidden in certain seasons.

pl-l4d33.summary: The patriarchs' polygamy was not sinful, being dispensed when God's worshippers were few and religion passed by blood; they sought offspring, not lust, and their marriages equal our virginity, Abraham having continence in habit as John had it in deed (c1–c2). The Law forbade unions with close kin and permitted divorce to prevent worse evils (c3); kings were allowed several wives, not many, but under grace marriage returned to one man and one woman, figuring Christ and the Church, with virginity preferred and continence enjoined on priests; virginity of mind surpasses that of flesh (c4).
claims: The patriarchs' polygamy was dispensed and not sinful.
Abraham's conjugal chastity equals John's virginity in merit.
Under grace marriage is monogamous, figuring Christ and the Church.
Virginity of mind surpasses virginity of flesh.

pl-l4d34.summary: Turns to lawful persons: some are fully lawful, some wholly unlawful by vow, order, kinship, or disparity of worship, and some intermediate by frigidity or servile condition (c1). Impotent spouses should live as brother and sister, though a wife who wants children may remarry after sworn proof (c2); impotence from sorcery is treated by penance and exorcism, separation following if incurable (c3). The insane cannot contract marriage, but later insanity does not dissolve it (c4). Intercourse with a spouse's sibling creates a lasting impediment (c5), and no illness or deformity justifies dismissing a spouse (c6).
claims: Impediments make persons wholly or partly unlawful for marriage.
Impotence may allow separation after proof.
Later insanity or illness does not dissolve marriage.
Intercourse with a spouse's sibling bars marriage.

pl-l4d35.summary: Wives as well as husbands may separate for fornication, adultery being condemned equally in both (c1), but a guilty spouse cannot dismiss a guilty one (c2). Separation for fornication does not permit remarriage; the spouses must remain continent or reconcile, and a repentant adulterous spouse may be received back, though keeping an unrepentant one is complicity (c3). Those who plotted or promised marriage during adultery may not marry, while penitent adulterers who did not may marry after the spouse's death (c4).
claims: Both spouses may separate for fornication.
Separation does not permit remarriage.
A repentant adulterous spouse may be received back.
Plotting or promising marriage during adultery bars that marriage.

pl-l4d36.summary: Error about servile condition allows separation, but knowing marriage to a slave is indissoluble (c1); masters may not dissolve slaves' marriages, though whether slaves can marry without their consent is disputed (c2); self-enslavement cannot dissolve marriage (c3). Boys must be fourteen and girls twelve to marry, child marriages binding if ratified after puberty, and espousals require age seven (c4).
claims: Unknown servile condition allows separation.
Masters may not dissolve slaves' marriages.
Minimum ages for marriage are fourteen and twelve.

pl-l4d37.summary: Major orders, subdiaconate, diaconate, and priesthood, invalidate marriage, and those in them must abstain from their wives; minor clerics may marry a virgin but cannot then advance (c1). Wife-killers are murderers denied marriage, and the Church punishes with the spiritual sword, not the material (c2).
claims: Major orders are a diriment impediment.
Minor clerics may marry but cannot advance.
Wife-killers are denied marriage; the Church wields only the spiritual sword.

pl-l4d38.summary: A vow is a spontaneous promise to God (c1). Vows are common or singular, private or solemn: a private vow of continence makes marriage sinful but valid, a solemn one invalidates it; vowed widows and virgins who marry are excommunicated and penanced; adultery, incest, and sin against nature are graded in gravity (c2). Wives who remarried believing their husbands dead must return to them, the second union excused by ignorance; a bigamist compelled by the Church to remain may render but never demand the debt (c3).
claims: A solemn vow of continence invalidates marriage; a private one makes it sinful.
Marriages contracted on presumption of death yield to the first.
Sin against nature is gravest among sexual sins.

pl-l4d39.summary: Disparity of worship bars marriage between Christians and unbelievers (c1). Paul's counsel concerns spouses married as unbelievers, one later converted, who may stay together; unbelief is spiritual fornication justifying separation, as is any corrupting concupiscence, but the believer is counseled to stay with a peaceable spouse (c2–c4). One deserted for the faith may remarry, but one who dismisses a willing spouse may not, and ratified marriages between believers are not dissolved by apostasy (c5). Unbelievers' marriage is true, lawful but not ratified (c6–c7).
claims: Disparity of worship invalidates marriage.
Unbelievers' marriage is lawful but not ratified.
A convert deserted for the faith may remarry.
Spiritual fornication may justify separation.

pl-l4d40.summary: Kinship is carnal or spiritual, and marriage is forbidden within the seventh degree of consanguinity and affinity (c1). Degrees are computed variously, six or seven depending on whether the trunk is counted, with the same result (c2), six matching the six ages of the world, seven the Church's union with Christ after this life (c3). Gregory's permission of the fourth degree was a special concession to the newly converted English (c4).
claims: Marriage is forbidden within the seventh degree of kinship.
Six- and seven-degree computations agree in substance.
Gregory's concession to the English was special.

pl-l4d41.summary: Affinity arises because spouses are one flesh, each's kin becoming kin to the other in the same degree, observed to the seventh degree (c1); lower limits in some authorities reflect the Church's dispensation, and affinity survives a spouse's death and extends to children of a second marriage (c2). Good-faith marriages within forbidden degrees are separated but their children are legitimate (c3), and kinship is proved by sworn witnesses or confession (c4). Lombard defines fornication, stuprum, adultery, incest, and rape (c5–c9).
claims: Affinity follows from one flesh and extends to the seventh degree.
The Church can dispense in remoter degrees.
Good-faith marriages within forbidden degrees have legitimate children.
Kinds of sexual sin are distinguished.

pl-l4d42.summary: Spiritual kinship, among sponsors, godchildren, the baptized, and penitents, is an impediment (c1); marrying a godchild or co-parent is forbidden, but sponsoring one's own or one's spouse's child after marriage does not dissolve it, harsher rulings being deterrents (c2). Spiritual children may not marry the sponsor's natural children, since spiritual kinship binds more than adoption (c3), though authorities differ on siblings born before or after (c4) and on marrying a late wife's co-mother, which depends on intercourse after the co-parenthood (c5); spouses should not sponsor the same child (c6). Successive marriages after a spouse's death are lawful, though bigamists are barred from orders for the sacrament's sign and second marriages lack the first's blessing (c7).
claims: Spiritual kinship is an impediment to marriage.
Sponsoring one's own child after marriage does not dissolve it.
Successive marriages are lawful.
Bigamists are barred from orders for the sake of the sacrament's sign.

pl-l4d43.summary: Turns to the last things: the flesh of all will rise, the dead in Christ first and the living caught up to meet him (c1), at the voice of the trumpet, Christ's or the angels' (c2), coming unexpectedly as at midnight (c3). The day of the Lord will reveal all consciences, each recalling all his deeds (c4); the blessed will remember past evils without pain but with gratitude, and sins covered by penance may remain hidden (c5). Whether those alive at the end will die and rise in the rapture cannot be decided (c6). All will rise whole and incorrupt, only the blessed impassible (c7).
claims: The flesh of all will rise.
At the judgment all consciences are revealed.
The blessed remember past evils with gratitude, not pain.
Whether the living die at Christ's coming is undecided.

pl-l4d44.summary: All will rise at the age of Christ's death, each with his own stature (c1), all bodily matter returning to its own soul though not necessarily to the same parts, as an artist remakes a statue (c2); the saints' bodies will rise without defect, shining and spiritual yet bodies (c3), while whether the damned keep their deformities is left open (c4). The damned's bodies will burn without being consumed (c5), demons will be tormented by bodily fire, whose nature and place are unknown (c6), and the souls of the reprobate already suffer fire, bearing a likeness of the body (c7). Formed fetuses will rise, and monsters with nature corrected (c8).
claims: All rise at Christ's age with their own stature.
Bodily matter returns to its soul, fittingly arranged.
The saints rise glorified; the damned burn without being consumed.
Hell's fire is bodily and torments demons and souls.

pl-l4d45.summary: Souls receive joy or torment at death, increased at the resurrection (c1). Suffrages help those who merited it in life: they bring full remission to the moderately good and mitigation to the moderately bad, the very good needing none and the very bad gaining nothing; martyrs are prayed to, not for (c2). Funeral pomp consoles the living, prayers help the dead (c3); special suffrages may hasten but not increase release (c4); those dying at the world's end are helped by the heavenly Church (c5). The saints know our petitions in the Word, as angels do, and intercede by merit and affection, willing only what God wills (c6).
claims: Suffrages help the dead who merited it in life.
Merit is acquired only in this life.
Martyrs are not prayed for.
The saints know our prayers in God and intercede.

pl-l4d46.summary: The damned's punishment is eternal, yet God, joining mercy to justice, punishes them less than they deserve (c1). God's hidden judgment purges, converts, or blinds, while the final judgment separates good and bad (c2). Justice and mercy are one divine essence, distinguished by their effects in creatures (c3); mercy frees from misery, goodness creates and governs all (c4). God's ways are his two comings, of mercy and of justice, and whether both appear in every work is disputed (c5).
claims: The damned are punished eternally but less than they deserve.
God's justice and mercy are one essence, distinguished by effects.
Mercy frees from misery; goodness extends to all.

pl-l4d47.summary: How the sentence will be pronounced is uncertain (c1). The saints, especially the perfect, will judge with Christ by authority (c2). There are four orders at the judgment: unbelievers condemned without examination, faithful sinners examined and condemned, ordinary elect examined and saved, and the perfect who judge (c3). The angels will gather and separate; a world-fire will transform the aerial heaven and purge the saints; the dead will rise, the good be caught up, and the wicked be cast into hell (c4). Whether demons will torment the damned is left open (c5).
claims: The saints will judge with Christ.
There are four orders at the judgment.
The angels minister at the judgment; a world-fire purges the world.

pl-l4d48.summary: Christ will judge in his glorified human form, seen by all, his divinity seen only by the pure of heart (c1–c2), raising bodies according to his humanity, whose passion and resurrection cause ours, though by divine power (c3). He will judge from the air above the Mount of Olives, the valley of Jehoshaphat signifying damnation (c4). The heavenly lights will be outshone at his coming and afterward shine more brightly and stand still, though their use then is unknown (c5).
claims: Christ judges in his glorified human form.
His humanity causes the resurrection of bodies.
The heavenly bodies will be renewed after the judgment.

pl-l4d49.summary: After the judgment the two cities reach their ends, with degrees of glory and punishment; all the elect enjoy God, the common denarius, by sight but unequally, the many mansions being degrees of vision; all will happiness, but only the blessed have all they will and will nothing badly (c1). All the blessed see the Trinity and all that pertains to beatitude, differing in clarity (c2); through charity their joy is shared, though their beatitude differs (c3). Beatitude increases after the judgment, since the separated soul is held back by its desire for the body and reaches perfection with a spiritual body (c4).
claims: Glory has degrees; all the elect enjoy God by sight.
Eternal life is knowing God.
The blessed share joy through charity.
Beatitude increases with the resurrection of the body.

pl-l4d50.summary: The damned keep an evil will that increases their punishment without merit, since merit and fruitful penance belong only to this life (c1). Their outer darkness is total separation from God's light, a growing hatred and forgetting of God amid torment (c2). The dead care for the living without necessarily knowing their affairs (c3); the details of the rich man and Lazarus are uncertain (c4); after the judgment only the blessed see the damned (c5) and, wholly devoted to God's justice, feel no compassion for them (c6), seeing their punishment with joy and gratitude for their own deliverance. Lombard ends the work, having passed from the face of him who sits on the throne to his feet, the Way leading (c7).
claims: The damned's evil will is punishment, not new merit.
Merit is possible only in this life.
Outer darkness is total separation from God.
The blessed see the damned without compassion and with gratitude.

pl-liber4.summary: Summary of Book 4 (on the sacraments and the last things), based on the prologue and all 50 distinctions. It remains partial at the chapter level: Distinctions 14, 19, 21, and 23 are divided differently in the TEI than in the EDF. The prologue turns from the doctrine of things to the doctrine of signs. Distinctions 1 and 2 define a sacrament as a sign of a sacred thing that bears its likeness and causes grace, distinguish the new sacraments, which give salvation, from the old, which only signified, and list the seven sacraments, which draw their power from Christ's passion. Distinctions 2 to 6 treat baptism: John's baptism, the form (the invocation of the Trinity), the matter (water), its institution at Christ's baptism, its reality (justification), who receives sacrament or reality or both, with martyrdom and faith with contrition supplying where necessity prevents it, since God is not bound to the sacraments; its validity whoever the minister, who has the ministry but not the power; and its rite, intention, and sponsors. Distinction 7 treats confirmation, reserved to bishops. Distinctions 8 to 13 treat the eucharist: its figures, institution, and form; its twofold reality, Christ's body and the Church's unity; sacramental and spiritual eating; the true presence of the whole Christ under each species by the conversion of bread and wine, whose accidents remain without a subject; the sacrifice as memorial and representation of the cross; and the validity of consecration by wicked priests but not, it seems, by heretics. Distinctions 14 to 22 treat penance: the second plank after shipwreck, both sacrament and virtue, repeatable; its three parts, contrition, confession, and satisfaction; the forgiveness of sin in contrition with the intention to confess, while confession to a priest who holds the keys remains required; the keys as declaring, imposing satisfaction, and excommunicating, God alone cleansing the soul; the purging of light sins after death; and the unresolved question whether forgiven sins return. Distinction 23 treats extreme unction. Distinctions 24 and 25 treat the seven orders and ordinations by heretics and simoniacs. Distinctions 26 to 42 treat marriage: instituted as duty and remedy, signifying Christ and the Church, made by free present consent and not by intercourse; its three goods, faith, offspring, and sacrament, which excuse intercourse; the equality of spouses in the debt; the dispensation of the patriarchs; and the impediments of impotence, adultery, servile condition, age, orders, vow, disparity of worship, consanguinity and affinity to the seventh degree, and spiritual kinship. Distinctions 43 to 50 treat the last things: the resurrection of all flesh at Christ's age and with its own matter; the revelation of consciences; suffrages for the dead, who are helped by the Church according to their merits; the eternal but mitigated punishment of the damned and the unity of God's mercy and justice; the order of the judgment, with the saints judging with Christ in his glorified human form; the renewal of the heavens; the degrees of glory in the vision of God; and the obstinacy and outer darkness of the damned, ending with the blessed's gratitude and the close of the work.
claims: Book 4 treats the sacraments as signs and remedies, and the last things.
A sacrament is a sign that bears the likeness of grace and causes it.
God instituted the sacraments but did not bind his power to them.
Baptism is valid with the Trinitarian form and water, whoever the minister.
In the eucharist bread and wine are converted into Christ's body and blood, and the whole Christ is under each species.
The eucharist is a sacrifice as memorial and representation of the cross.
Sin is forgiven in contrition with the intention to confess; confession to a priest is required when possible.
God alone cleanses the soul; priests bind and loose through the keys.
Marriage is made by free present consent and signifies the union of Christ and the Church.
Marriage has three goods: faith, offspring, and sacrament.
Kinship and affinity forbid marriage to the seventh degree.
The flesh of all will rise, and Christ will judge in his glorified human form.
Suffrages help the dead who merited it in life.
The blessed enjoy God by sight in degrees of glory; the damned suffer eternally.

_metadata.note: All 51 direct children (the prologue and 50 distinctions) are covered, but Distinction 14, Distinction 19, Distinction 21, Distinction 23 are themselves partial

lombardsententia.summary: Partial summary of Peter Lombard's Sentences, based on all of Liber 1, Liber 2 (all distinctions; one chapter pending and two distinctions divided differently than in the EDF), all of Liber 3, and all of Liber 4 (four distinctions divided differently than in the EDF). The prologue and opening distinction give the plan of the work: a compilation of the Fathers' sentences in four books, organized by things and signs, with the Trinity as the sole object of enjoyment, moving from God through creatures and Christ to the sacraments as signs. Lombard assembles and harmonizes scriptural and patristic authorities, above all Augustine and Hilary, often by distinguishing senses or confessing the limits of understanding. Book 1, now fully interpreted, presents the one simple, immutable God in three coequal persons; the generation of the Son and procession of the Spirit; the missions and the Spirit as the charity by which we love; an extended analysis of divine names, persons, properties, and relations; and God's knowledge, foreknowledge, predestination, power, and will, which is always fulfilled and permits but does not author evil. Book 2 treats creation from nothing by God's goodness; the creation, fall, confirmation, and orders of angels; the work of the six days; man as image of the Trinity, the soul's creation, paradise, and the original state ordered to merit by obedience; the fall; free choice, grace, and merit against the Pelagians; original sin and its remission in baptism; actual sin, evil as privation, will, intention, and the morality of acts; the capital vices and the sin against the Holy Spirit; and God's sovereignty over all power together with the moral limits of obedience. Book 3 treats man's restoration through the Mediator: only the Son became incarnate, assuming whole human nature but not a human person, with Lombard reporting three opinions on the union without deciding; Christ's grace, knowledge, defects, two wills, and merit; the redemption through his death, in which neither soul nor flesh was parted from the Word; faith, hope, and charity, the cardinal virtues, and the gifts of the Spirit, all connected in charity; and the Decalogue, fulfilled in the two commandments of charity, with treatments of lying and perjury. Book 4 turns to the doctrine of signs and the last things: the sacraments as signs that bear the likeness of grace and cause it, instituted by God though he is not bound to them; baptism and confirmation; the eucharist, in which bread and wine are converted into Christ's body and blood, a sacrifice as memorial of the cross whose further reality is the Church's unity; penance, in which sin is forgiven in contrition while confession to priests who hold the keys remains required, with unfinished satisfaction completed in purgatorial fire; extreme unction and the seven orders; marriage, made by free present consent, signifying Christ and the Church, with its three goods and its impediments; and the resurrection of the body, suffrages for the dead, the judgment by Christ in his glorified humanity, the vision of God in degrees of glory, and the eternal punishment of the damned. The work ends, as it says, having passed from the face of him who sits on the throne through the middle to his feet.
claims: The Sentences compile the Fathers' sentences in four books, organized by things and signs.
Lombard resolves questions by collating and harmonizing patristic and scriptural authorities, chiefly Augustine.
God is one simple, immutable essence in three coeternal and coequal persons, distinguished by relations of origin.
The Holy Spirit is the charity by which God loves and by which we love God.
God's foreknowledge, predestination, power, and will are without necessity on creatures, merit, or authorship of evil.
Divine causality of power and immutable presence are maintained alongside creaturely responsibility.
Faith formed by charity, whether explicit or implicit, is necessary for salvation.
The Word assumed human nature, not a human person; Christ redeemed us by his death, conquering the devil by justice.
Charity, the Holy Spirit, is one love of God and neighbor and the fulfilment of the Decalogue.
Sacraments are signs that cause the grace they signify; in the eucharist bread and wine are converted into Christ's body and blood.
Sin is forgiven in contrition with the intention to confess, and priests bind and loose through the keys.
Marriage is made by free consent in words of the present and signifies the union of Christ and the Church.
The flesh of all will rise; Christ will judge in his glorified humanity; the blessed will see God in degrees of glory and the damned suffer eternally.

_metadata.note: All four books have interpretations, but Liber 2 and Liber 4 are themselves partial
